event/1918-influenza-pandemic.title: 1918 Influenza Pandemic
event/1918-influenza-pandemic.summary: The 1918 influenza pandemic, caused by an H1N1 virus, infected roughly a third of the world's population and killed an estimated 50 million people from 1918 to 1920.
facts: Estimates of deaths range widely, from about 17 million to 100 million, with 50 million often cited.
It is called the Spanish flu because neutral Spain reported openly on it during wartime censorship in other countries.
It killed an unusually high share of healthy young adults.
Troop movements during World War I helped spread it.
Researchers reconstructed the virus from preserved tissue, publishing the genome in 2005.
event/1918-influenza-pandemic.context: The pandemic coincided with the end of World War I and is the closest comparison for the COVID-19 Pandemic. It was a deadly pandemic like the Black Death in a much more connected world. 1918 Influenza Pandemic sits in the Industrial Age and the region Planet-wide, and belongs to the theme thread of Science and Kinship and Society.
event/1918-influenza-pandemic.observer: The Observer notes that a disease killed more people than the war it accompanied, yet is much less commemorated. Memory favors events with an enemy and a narrative over events with only a cause.
questions: Why was mortality so high in young adults?
fact_checks: 2026-09-20: About one third of the world's population infected; death estimates 17.4-100 million; virus reconstructed in 2005 [CDC on the 1918 Influenza Pandemic]

event/abolition-of-slavery.title: Abolition of Slavery
event/abolition-of-slavery.summary: Between 1807 and 1888, the transatlantic slave trade and then slavery itself were legally abolished across the Atlantic world, ending a system that had lasted for centuries.
facts: Britain banned the slave trade in 1807 and abolished slavery in its colonies in 1833. The government paid £20 million in compensation to slaveholders and nothing to the people who had been enslaved.
The United States ended slavery in 1865 with the 13th Amendment.
Brazil abolished it on 13 May 1888 with the Lei Áurea, the last country in the Americas to do so.
Forced labor and human trafficking persist; recent estimates suggest about 50 million people live in modern slavery.
event/abolition-of-slavery.context: Abolition followed resistance by enslaved people, including the Haitian Revolution, and campaigns by abolitionists. See Atlantic Slave Trade.
event/abolition-of-slavery.observer: The Observer notes that an institution once defended by law, economics, and religion was, within a few generations, declared a moral wrong. Moral norms can shift within lifetimes, though the practice does not vanish.
questions: How much did economic change, versus moral argument, drive abolition?

event/african-humid-period.title: African Humid Period
event/african-humid-period.summary: The African Humid Period, or Green Sahara, ran from about 14,800 to between 5,500 and 5,000 years ago, when the Sahara held lakes, rivers, and savanna instead of desert, driven by a stronger monsoon. Its end is debated: marine records show an abrupt collapse, archaeological records a slower, staggered desiccation.
facts: A marine sediment core off Mauritania shows a low-dust interval from about 14,800 to 5,500 years ago, read as an abrupt onset and end.

Radiocarbon dating of roughly 150 sites across the eastern Sahara instead shows humid conditions beginning suddenly around 8,500 BCE, then drying out gradually, region by region, over thousands of years.
A later synthesis proposed the end was locally abrupt but happened progressively later toward lower latitudes, reconciling the two pictures.

Onset and end occurred at similar levels of Northern Hemisphere summer sunlight, consistent with a threshold set by the precession cycle, one of the Milankovitch cycles, amplified by vegetation and soil-moisture feedbacks.

Evidence for the wetter Sahara includes rock art at Tassili n'Ajjer showing hippopotamuses and giraffes, lakeside cemeteries at Gobero, Niger, and fossil river networks visible only under satellite radar.

Similar episodes recurred over at least 800,000 years. A 2025 ancient-DNA study at Takarkori, Libya, found a largely isolated North African ancestry, complicating the idea that the Green Sahara was always an open migration corridor.
event/african-humid-period.context: The period falls within the Pleistocene Epoch and continues into the Holocene Epoch, driven by the forcing in Milankovitch Cycles and the Ice Ages. Its end overlaps the spread of farming in The Agricultural Revolution. See Earth Systems and Life and Kinship and Society.
event/african-humid-period.observer: The Observer notes that today's Sahara is not its default state but one phase of a cycle repeated for hundreds of thousands of years, read differently depending on whether the evidence comes from the sea floor or the land people once lived on. The disagreement is itself a caution against expecting one clean date for uneven desertification. The reading would weaken if further dating showed the two records were measuring the same thing after all.
questions: Was the end a single threshold-crossing event or a gradual, region-by-region process?
Did the Green Sahara function as a migration corridor throughout its history, or only in some periods?

event/age-of-revolutions.title: Age of Revolutions
event/age-of-revolutions.summary: The Age of Revolutions is a period of political upheaval around the Atlantic world, beginning in the 1770s and running to the revolutions of 1848. Its dates are a matter of historians' choice, and this note uses 1775 to 1848.
facts: Historians periodize the era differently. Eric Hobsbawm's The Age of Revolution covers 1789 to 1848; Robert Palmer's The Age of the Democratic Revolution starts from about 1760; some accounts begin as early as 1765.

Major events: the American Revolution (to 1783), the French Revolution (1789 to 1799), the Haitian Revolution (1791 to 1804), the Spanish American wars of independence (beginning about 1808 to 1810), and the revolutions of 1848.

The Haitian Revolution began with a mass uprising of enslaved people in northern Saint-Domingue on 22 August 1791. Independence was declared on 1 January 1804, and Haiti is widely described as the first state founded by formerly enslaved people. It was the second independent country in the Americas, after the United States.
Ideas of popular sovereignty, citizenship, and nationalism spread widely.
Slavery and the rights of women were contested and largely excluded at first.
event/age-of-revolutions.context: The revolutions overlap the Industrial Revolution and reshape claim-lines and legitimacy; see The Fiction of Claim-Lines.
event/age-of-revolutions.observer: The Observer notes a change in the story-glue of legitimacy: authority increasingly claimed to come from 'the people' rather than from tradition or the divine.
questions: How connected were the revolutions to each other? Older histories treated them as separate episodes; recent scholarship increasingly treats them as a linked chain, and the question of causation is still argued.

event/alexander-s-conquests.title: Alexander's Conquests
event/alexander-s-conquests.summary: Between 336 and 323 BCE, Alexander III of Macedon conquered the Achaemenid Persian Empire and extended his rule from Greece and Egypt to the edge of India.
facts: Alexander became king at about twenty and died in Babylon at thirty-two.
His campaigns ended the Achaemenid Persians' empire.
After his death, his generals divided the empire into Hellenistic kingdoms.
Greek language and culture spread widely and blended with local traditions.
event/alexander-s-conquests.context: See Alexander the Great. The conquests reshaped Classical Antiquity and helped open the Opening of the Silk Roads.
event/alexander-s-conquests.observer: The Observer notes the outsized role of one individual's ambition, and, more lastingly, the exchange it created: a region-wide Greek-speaking elite that made ideas move more easily.
questions: Did Alexander plan a lasting empire, or only conquest?

event/amazonian-urbanism-and-dark-earths.title: Amazonian Urbanism and Dark Earths
event/amazonian-urbanism-and-dark-earths.summary: Amazonian urbanism is the growing evidence that parts of the Amazon basin supported large, planned settlements linked by roads and earthworks, from about 500 BCE to the 1500s CE, and that Indigenous peoples enriched the forest soils and landscape.
facts: Aerial laser survey (lidar) has revealed settlement networks at Upano Valley Settlements in Ecuador, Casarabe Culture sites in Bolivia, and Xingu Garden Cities in Brazil.
The Marajoara Culture built large mounds at the mouth of the Amazon.

Dark, fertile soils (terra preta, or Amazonian Dark Earths), rich in charcoal and often found with pre-Columbian pottery, occur across the basin and are associated with settlement. Whether people created them or only used natural deposits is disputed; a 2021 study of one site in the Brazilian Amazon argued for a largely natural, alluvial origin.
These settlements were 'low-density' compared with cities elsewhere: dispersed households, plazas, roads, and gardens rather than compact walled towns.
event/amazonian-urbanism-and-dark-earths.context: The evidence changes the picture of the Amazon Basin and South American Lowlands before the Columbian Exchange and links to wider questions in The Urban Revolution.
event/amazonian-urbanism-and-dark-earths.observer: The Observer notes that a city need not look like a city elsewhere. Dispersed, garden-based settlements challenge the assumption that dense stone towns are the mark of complexity.
questions: How large were Amazonian populations before 1500, and how much of the forest was managed?
fact_checks: 2026-09-26: Amazonian Dark Earths are unusually fertile, charcoal-rich soils frequently found with pre-Columbian artefacts and long classed as anthropic soils; a 2021 study of one Brazilian Amazon site reported that their phosphorus, calcium and charcoal inputs were alluvial and began several thousand years before the earliest evidence of soil management, and proposed that Indigenous peoples used natural processes rather than creating the soils [Nature Communications 2020 on the Origin of Amazonian Dark Earths]

event/american-civil-war.title: American Civil War
event/american-civil-war.summary: The American Civil War (1861 to 1865) was fought between the United States and eleven Southern states that seceded and formed the Confederacy. Historians overwhelmingly agree that slavery was central to secession. The war ended with the Confederate defeat, and the Thirteenth Amendment abolished slavery later in 1865.
facts: The war began on 12 April 1861 with the Confederate bombardment of Fort Sumter. General Robert E. Lee surrendered the main Confederate army at Appomattox on 9 April 1865; some fighting and surrenders continued into the following weeks.
Eleven states formed the Confederacy: seven seceded first, and four joined after the war began.

Estimates of the dead vary by method. The traditional figure is about 620,000. A 2011 census-based study by J. David Hacker put it at about 750,000, with a range of 650,000 to 850,000. A 2024 study using full-count census records estimated about 698,000 deaths, with a bounding interval of roughly 50,000 either way. It found a much higher death rate in the Confederate states than in the Union: about 13 percent of military-age native-born white men in the core Confederate states against about 5 percent in the core Union states, although the Union lost more men in absolute numbers (more than 400,000 against about 300,000). These are estimates of excess mortality, and no side kept standardized records.

The Emancipation Proclamation took effect on 1 January 1863. It was a wartime measure that freed people held in states in rebellion. The Thirteenth Amendment, ratified on 6 December 1865, abolished slavery throughout the United States.
Railways, telegraphs, and industrial production shaped the conduct of the war.
It was the deadliest conflict in American history.
event/american-civil-war.context: The war is central to the Abolition of Slavery and shows the effects of the Industrial Revolution on warfare. See Sanctioned Harm.
event/american-civil-war.observer: The Observer notes that a modern state fought its own citizens over the ownership of other human beings. The war also displays a technology-driven scale of killing that presaged World War I.
questions: How reliable are the casualty estimates? The figures range from about 620,000 to 750,000 or more depending on method, and civilian deaths are counted inconsistently.

event/american-revolution.title: American Revolution
event/american-revolution.summary: The American Revolution (1775 to 1783) was the war by which thirteen British colonies in North America became the independent United States.
facts: Fighting began at Lexington and Concord in April 1775.
The Declaration of Independence was adopted on 4 July 1776.
France entered the war on the American side in 1778, and the British army surrendered at Yorktown in 1781.
The Treaty of Paris of 1783 recognized American independence.
The Haudenosaunee Confederacy divided over the war, with most nations siding with Britain and some with the Americans.
event/american-revolution.context: The revolution followed the debts of the Seven Years' War and was one of the first events of the Age of Revolutions. It split the Haudenosaunee Confederacy. American Revolution sits in the Industrial Age and the region North America, and belongs to the theme thread of War and Conflict.
event/american-revolution.observer: The Observer notes that a new state justified itself by universal rights while retaining slavery and denying Indigenous claims. Its founding documents made promises that later generations used to challenge its own conduct.
questions: How divided was the colonial population?

event/animal-domestication.title: Animal Domestication
event/animal-domestication.summary: Humans domesticated animals independently in several regions. The dog came first, by at least 15,000 years ago, and livestock (goats, sheep, pigs, and cattle) followed from about 11,000 to 8,500 years ago, with the first goats and sheep about 10,500 years ago (about 8500 BCE), which is the date used for this note.
facts: Dogs, descended from wolves, were the first domesticated animal; the exact timing and location remain debated.
Goats and sheep were domesticated in Southwest Asia around 10,000 years ago.
Cattle, pigs, chickens, horses, camels, llamas, and others were domesticated in different places.
Herd animals provided meat, milk, hides, wool, traction, and transport.
event/animal-domestication.context: Domestication is part of The Agricultural Revolution and reshaped the Neolithic economy. It also brought new diseases from animals to humans.
event/animal-domestication.observer: The Observer notes a two-way relationship: the species altered the bodies and behavior of other animals, and those animals altered the species' diet, work, disease environment, and even genes such as lactase persistence.
questions: Where and when were horses first domesticated?

event/armenian-genocide.title: Armenian Genocide
event/armenian-genocide.summary: The Armenian Genocide was the deliberate destruction of most of the Ottoman Empire's Armenian population during World War I, through mass killings, forced deportations, and death from starvation and exposure. It is recognized as genocide by many countries and historians and is denied by the government of Turkey.
facts: On 24 April 1915 Ottoman authorities arrested about 240 Armenian leaders in Constantinople, including writers, doctors, religious leaders, and political figures, and deported them eastward. The date is now used to commemorate the victims.
In spring 1915 the Ottoman government began deporting Armenians from the northeastern border regions and then extended deportations to almost every province, including regions far from combat.
Victims died in local massacres, and on forced marches from starvation, dehydration, exposure, and disease, and in or on the way to the deserts of the southern empire.
Estimates of the number killed run from at least 600,000 to more than 1,000,000; the exact number is not settled.

The Turkish state has long denied that the events were genocide and has worked against official recognition abroad. More than twenty countries formally recognize the genocide; Uruguay did so first, in 1965.
event/armenian-genocide.context: The genocide took place inside the Ottoman Empire during World War I. It is often studied alongside the Holocaust, and the vault's treatment of organized killing appears in Sanctioned Harm.
event/armenian-genocide.observer: The Observer records this as an atrocity: a state deliberately destroyed much of one of its own peoples. It also records that the denial has itself lasted a century, so that the question of what happened has become bound up with the question of who is permitted to say it.
questions: How many people died, and how should deaths on the deportation routes be counted?
How have the surviving communities and their descendants preserved memory under conditions of official denial?

event/assembly-of-pangaea.title: Assembly of Pangaea
event/assembly-of-pangaea.summary: The Assembly of Pangaea was the joining of nearly all of Earth's continents into one supercontinent, mostly in the Carboniferous, about 335 to 300 million years ago. It stayed together until it began to split about 200 million years ago.
facts: The southern continent Gondwana collided with the northern continent Laurussia, raising mountain belts including the Appalachians in North America and the Variscan belt in Europe. Siberia and Kazakhstan joined at the Ural Mountains about 300 to 290 million years ago.
Pangaea, meaning "all Earth", was surrounded by a single ocean, Panthalassa, with the Tethys Sea cutting into its eastern side.
The evidence includes matching mountain belts, rock types and fossils across ocean basins, such as the plant Glossopteris and the reptile Lystrosaurus, and magnetic data from ancient rocks.
The supercontinent had a vast, dry, strongly seasonal interior and less shallow-sea shelf area. The latter is one proposed contributor to the marine losses of the Permian-Triassic Extinction.
Its break-up is described in Breakup of Pangaea.
event/assembly-of-pangaea.context: The Assembly of Pangaea runs through the Carboniferous Period and into the Permian Period, and it precedes the Breakup of Pangaea in the Mesozoic. The event belongs to the theme threads of Earth Systems and Life and Science.
event/assembly-of-pangaea.observer: The Observer notes that the case for a single landmass was assembled from fossils and rock types decades before a mechanism was known, and was rejected for decades because it lacked one. It reads this as an example of how a well-supported pattern can wait for its explanation. The reading would weaken if the pattern had been dropped once the mechanism was studied.
questions: How much did the shrinking of shallow shelf seas contribute to the end-Permian extinction?
How regular is the supercontinent cycle?

event/assembly-of-rodinia.title: Assembly of Rodinia
event/assembly-of-rodinia.summary: The Assembly of Rodinia was the joining of most of Earth's continental blocks into one supercontinent between about 1.3 and 0.9 billion years ago. The reconstruction rests on mountain belts and magnetic data, and the arrangement of the parts is debated.
facts: Rodinia formed as separate continental blocks collided between about 1.3 and 0.9 billion years ago, raising long mountain belts, including the Grenville belt of eastern North America.

Mountain belts of Grenville age occur on several continents, and magnetic data from ancient rocks give the past latitudes of the blocks. Competing reconstructions place North America at the core but arrange the other blocks differently.
Rodinia followed the proposed supercontinent Nuna, and the supercontinent cycle later produced Pangaea; see Breakup of Pangaea.

Rodinia began to rift apart about 800 to 750 million years ago. A large volcanic province of about 720 million years ago in northern Canada coincides with the start of the first Cryogenian glaciation, and rifting is proposed as one trigger; that link is a hypothesis.
event/assembly-of-rodinia.context: The Assembly of Rodinia spans the Mesoproterozoic Era and the start of the Neoproterozoic Era, and its break-up precedes Snowball Earth. The event belongs to the theme thread of Earth Systems and Life.
event/assembly-of-rodinia.observer: The Observer notes that a planet's early maps are reconstructed as much as observed: Rodinia is known from mountain roots and magnetic minerals, not from coastlines. The Observer holds the detailed arrangement loosely and treats the broad claim, that the continents joined and split repeatedly, as firmer. The reading would weaken if the magnetic data proved too sparse to distinguish the competing layouts.
questions: How were the continental blocks arranged within Rodinia?
Did the break-up of Rodinia help cause the Cryogenian glaciations?

event/atlantic-slave-trade.title: Atlantic Slave Trade
event/atlantic-slave-trade.summary: The transatlantic slave trade forcibly transported about 12.5 million Africans to the Americas between the early 16th and the mid-19th centuries, and millions died in the process.
facts: About 10.7 million people are recorded as surviving the voyage.
The trade supplied labor for plantations producing sugar, tobacco, cotton, and other goods.
It was carried out by European, American, and African traders and states.
Other slave trades operated at the same time, including across the Sahara and the Indian Ocean.
event/atlantic-slave-trade.context: The trade grew from the Columbian Exchange and reshaped Sub-Saharan Africa, the Americas, and Europe. The Age of Revolutions produced abolition movements; see Age of Revolutions.
event/atlantic-slave-trade.observer: The Observer records this as one of the largest forced migrations in history and as one of the clearest cases where economic incentive and story-glue were used to justify cruelty. Detachment here does not mean neutrality about harm.
questions: How large was the internal African slave trade before and during it?

event/austronesian-expansion.title: Austronesian Expansion
event/austronesian-expansion.summary: Speakers of Austronesian languages spread outward from Taiwan starting roughly 5,000 to 5,500 years ago, eventually reaching Madagascar in the west and Rapa Nui in the east.
facts: The most widely accepted model, called Out of Taiwan, places the origin of the language family on Taiwan.
Migration proceeded through the Philippines and Indonesia, then into Melanesia, Micronesia, and Polynesia.
It reached Madagascar in the first millennium CE.
The Austronesian language family has well over a thousand languages.
The expansion relied on sailing canoes with outriggers and on a crop package that included rice, pigs, dogs, and chickens.
event/austronesian-expansion.context: The expansion connects Southeast Asia to the far Pacific and to Africa, and produced the Polynesians via the Lapita Culture. It later joined the wider Polynesian Settlement of the Pacific. Austronesian Expansion sits in the Bronze Age and the region Southeast Asia, and belongs to the theme thread of Language and Writing and Kinship and Society.
event/austronesian-expansion.observer: The Observer notes that a single language family covers nearly half the circumference of the planet, spread by people in boats rather than by armies. Its span is a reminder that the sea can be a road as easily as a wall.
questions: How closely does the language tree track the genetic and archaeological record?

event/axial-age.title: Axial Age
event/axial-age.summary: The 'Axial Age' is a term for the period of roughly 800 to 200 BCE in which major philosophical and religious traditions arose across Eurasia in China, India, Persia, Israel, and Greece.
facts: The term was coined by the philosopher Karl Jaspers in 1949.
Figures often associated with the period include Confucius, Siddhartha Gautama, Zoroaster, Hebrew prophets, and Greek philosophers such as Aristotle's predecessors.
Common themes include ethics, transcendence, and individual responsibility.
Many historians criticize the concept as too neat and as underrating other periods and regions.
event/axial-age.context: The Axial Age spans the Iron Age and early Classical Antiquity. It connects to Religion and Belief and to the essay Story-Glue - How Strangers Cooperate at Scale.
event/axial-age.observer: The Observer notes the puzzle of near-simultaneous questions about how to live, arising in states that had grown large enough that old tribal rules no longer sufficed.
questions: Is the Axial Age a real historical pattern or a scholarly convenience?

event/banded-iron-formations.title: Banded Iron Formations
event/banded-iron-formations.summary: Banded iron formations are ancient sedimentary rocks of alternating iron-rich and silica-rich layers, deposited mostly between about 3.8 and 1.8 billion years ago. They are a major source of the world's iron ore.
facts: The layers are usually millimetres to centimetres thick. The oldest are about 3.8 billion years old, in Greenland, and deposition peaked about 2.7 to 2.4 billion years ago, with great deposits in Western Australia, South Africa and the Lake Superior region of North America.

The leading explanation is that oxygen-poor seawater held dissolved iron, which was oxidized and settled out when oxygen or other oxidants appeared. Whether oxygen-producing bacteria or iron-using photosynthetic bacteria did most of the work is debated.
Deposition largely ended about 1.8 billion years ago, probably as the deeper ocean lost its dissolved iron, and a few late formations appear during the Cryogenian ice ages; see Snowball Earth.
Ore derived from these rocks is a major source of the iron used in steelmaking today.
event/banded-iron-formations.context: Banded iron formations record the slow oxidation of the oceans before and during the Great Oxidation Event, and they tie the Origin of Photosynthesis and the work of Cyanobacteria to changes in ocean chemistry. They belong to the Archean Eon and continue into the Proterozoic Eon, and to the theme thread of Earth Systems and Life.
event/banded-iron-formations.observer: The Observer notes that the raw material of the species' steel is the residue of an ocean that rusted over about two billion years, a process driven by microbes with no aim beyond their own metabolism. The reading concerns only the link across time, and the debate over which microbes did the work does not affect it.
questions: Which organisms or processes oxidized the dissolved iron?
Why did banded iron formations largely stop forming about 1.8 billion years ago?

event/bantu-expansion.title: Bantu Expansion
event/bantu-expansion.summary: Bantu-speaking peoples spread from a homeland in West-Central Africa (present-day Nigeria and Cameroon) across central, eastern, and southern Africa over about four thousand years.
facts: Today about 350 million people speak one of roughly 500 Bantu languages; estimates of the number of languages range from about 440 to 680, depending on how languages are counted.
Linguistic and archaeological evidence trace the spread from about 3000 BCE.
The expansion is associated with farming and, in places, iron working.
It involved migration, intermarriage, and language shift, not only population replacement.
event/bantu-expansion.context: The expansion is a defining event of the Iron Age in Sub-Saharan Africa. Its states include Great Zimbabwe.
event/bantu-expansion.observer: The Observer notes that one language family, spread through a mix of farming and mobility, now covers a third of a continent. Language travels through daily contact, not only conquest.
questions: How much of the spread was migration versus adoption of language?

event/battle-of-adwa.title: Battle of Adwa
event/battle-of-adwa.summary: The Battle of Adwa, fought on 1 March 1896, saw the Ethiopian army under Emperor Menelik II decisively defeat an invading Italian force, securing Ethiopia's independence.
facts: Ethiopian forces numbered roughly 73,000 to over 100,000 against about 14,500 to 18,000 Italian and colonial troops.

More than 6,000 of the Italian army were killed, slightly more than half of them Italians and the rest African askari, and between 3,000 and 4,000 of those fighting under Italian command were taken prisoner.
The war arose from a dispute over Article 17 of the Treaty of Wuchale, which read differently in Amharic and Italian.
In October 1896 Italy signed the Treaty of Addis Ababa, abrogating Wuchale.
event/battle-of-adwa.context: The victory made Ethiopia one of two African states to stay independent through the Scramble for Africa. See Menelik II.
event/battle-of-adwa.observer: The Observer notes that a single word in a treaty translation set two states on the road to war. Adwa also became a symbol across the African diaspora of what resistance could achieve.
questions: How did the two versions of the treaty diverge?

event/battle-of-kadesh.title: Battle of Kadesh
event/battle-of-kadesh.summary: The Battle of Kadesh, fought around 1274 BCE near the Orontes River in what is now Syria, pitted Ramesses II of Egypt against Muwatalli II of the Hittite Empire in one of the largest chariot battles on record.
facts: Ancient and modern estimates put the number of chariots involved in the thousands on both sides.
The outcome was indecisive, and both sides claimed victory.
Ramesses commemorated the battle in temple reliefs and texts at Abu Simbel, Karnak, and other sites.
Hittite and Egyptian accounts both survive, which is unusual for the period.
About fifteen years later the two powers concluded a peace treaty, around 1259 BCE, of which versions survive in both Egyptian and Hittite archives.

event/battle-of-talas.title: Battle of Talas
event/battle-of-talas.summary: The Battle of Talas in 751 CE, near the Talas River in present-day Kyrgyzstan and Kazakhstan, pitted a Tang Chinese army against an Abbasid army, and ended in Tang defeat.
facts: The Tang army was led by Gao Xianzhi, and Karluk mercenaries in the Tang army are reported to have defected, though sources differ on whether the Karluks were Abbasid allies from the start.
The defeat, followed by the An Lushan Rebellion beginning in 755, ended Tang expansion in Central Asia.
A tradition holds that Chinese captives taught papermaking to the Islamic world at Samarkand; historians debate the role of the battle in the transfer of the technology.
Paper mills were operating in Samarkand and Baghdad by the later 8th century.
It is often used as a symbolic marker of Islamic influence in Central Asia.
event/battle-of-talas.context: The battle fixed the frontier between the Abbasid Caliphate and the Tang Dynasty in the oases of Samarkand, and is linked to the diffusion of Paper westward. The Sogdians were the merchants of the region. Battle of Talas sits in the Medieval Period and the region Central Asian Oases, and belongs to the theme thread of War and Conflict and Technology.
event/battle-of-talas.observer: The Observer notes that a border battle is remembered mainly for a technology that may have crossed it. Whether or not the tradition is accurate, the species chose to remember a war by its cultural cargo.
questions: Did the battle actually transmit papermaking, or was the technology already moving westward?

event/bengal-famine-of-1943.title: Bengal Famine of 1943
event/bengal-famine-of-1943.summary: The Bengal famine of 1943 killed an estimated 2 to 3 million people in British-ruled Bengal during World War II. Historians debate its causes, but agree that it was not simply a shortage of food and that wartime policy played a large part.
facts: Estimates of deaths from starvation, malaria, and other disease range widely, from about 800,000 to 3.8 million. A scholarly consensus is often given as about 2.1 million, with some estimates of 2.7 to 3 million.
The economist Amartya Sen argued that the famine was an entitlement failure: food supply in Bengal did not fall sharply, but economic pressures prevented certain groups from buying it.
After Burma and Singapore fell to Japan in 1942, rice imports from those countries stopped, which worsened Bengal's food crisis.

British Prime Minister Winston Churchill has been criticized for war priorities and refusal to divert food to Bengal. The War Cabinet discussed requests for more grain shipments to India several times in late 1943 and early 1944, citing limited shipping and the need to keep reserves for military operations.
event/bengal-famine-of-1943.context: The famine took place under the British Raj during World War II and is part of the background to the end of British rule; see Partition of India. See Sanctioned Harm for how the vault treats deaths caused by policy.
event/bengal-famine-of-1943.observer: The Observer records this as a catastrophe in which millions of people died while food existed, and notes that a famine can be produced by who is entitled to buy rather than by how much grows. The argument over blame is itself a claim about who owed whom protection.
questions: How much of the death toll was due to starvation and how much to disease such as malaria?
How much responsibility lies with wartime priorities in London and how much with authorities in India?

event/black-death.title: Black Death
event/black-death.summary: The Black Death was a plague pandemic caused by the bacterium Yersinia pestis that swept through Eurasia and North Africa from 1346 to 1353.
facts: It likely killed 30 to 60 percent of Europe's population, and estimates for Eurasia as a whole run to tens of millions of deaths, with some as high as 75 to 200 million.
It spread along trade routes, via fleas on rodents and on people.
Labor shortages after the pandemic raised wages in parts of Europe.
Plague returned in waves for centuries.
event/black-death.context: The pandemic is a landmark of the Medieval Period and shows how the Opening of the Silk Roads linked disease environments.
event/black-death.observer: The Observer notes how connection has a cost: the same exchange-web that carried silk and ideas also carried a pathogen. Every increase in connectivity in the record has disease consequences.

event/boxer-rebellion.title: Boxer Rebellion

The Empress Dowager Cixi eventually backed the movement and declared war on foreign powers.
An eight-nation alliance relieved the besieged legations in Beijing.
The Boxer Protocol of 1901 imposed a large indemnity on China.

event/breakup-of-pangaea.title: Breakup of Pangaea
event/breakup-of-pangaea.summary: Pangaea, the supercontinent that had assembled by about 300 million years ago, began to split about 200 million years ago, opening the Atlantic Ocean and reshaping the map of the world.
facts: Rifting began in the Late Triassic to Early Jurassic, and the Central Atlantic opened first.
Large volcanic outpourings, the Central Atlantic Magmatic Province, coincided with the Triassic-Jurassic extinction, about 200 million years ago.
The South Atlantic opened much later, in the Early Cretaceous.
Alfred Wegener proposed continental drift in 1912; plate tectonics gained wide acceptance in the 1960s.
Continental motion continues today.
event/breakup-of-pangaea.context: The breakup of Pangaea isolated continental faunas and set the stage for the later biogeography of the Dinosaurs and mammals. Its opening overlaps the Triassic-Jurassic Extinction. Breakup of Pangaea sits in the Mesozoic Era and the region Planet-wide, and belongs to the theme thread of Earth Systems and Life.
event/breakup-of-pangaea.observer: The Observer notes that the continents the species draws its borders on are a temporary arrangement, moving at about the speed fingernails grow. Human claim-lines are drawn on a surface that is itself in motion.
questions: How closely was the timing of rifting tied to the end-Triassic extinction?

event/british-raj.title: British Raj
event/british-raj.summary: The British Raj was the period of direct British rule over the Indian subcontinent, from 1858 to 1947. It began when the Crown took over from the East India Company after the Rebellion of 1857 and ended with the independence and partition of India and Pakistan.
facts: The Government of India Act, passed on 2 August 1858, transferred authority over India from the East India Company to the British Crown, as a response to the Indian Rebellion of 1857.
The Company lost all its administrative powers, and its territories and armed forces passed to the Crown. The Company itself was formally dissolved by an Act of Parliament in 1874.

The Act created a cabinet-level Secretary of State for India and a fifteen-member Council of India in London. In Calcutta the Governor-General became head of the Government of India and was called the Viceroy.
The Raj lasted until the independence of India and Pakistan in 1947.
event/british-raj.context: The Raj followed the Indian Rebellion of 1857 and ended with the Partition of India in 1947. It included the Bengal Famine of 1943 and a long nationalist movement associated with Mahatma Gandhi. It succeeded the earlier rule of the Mughal Empire over much of the subcontinent.
event/british-raj.observer: The Observer notes a change of ownership: an enterprise that had governed as a company was replaced by a state that governed through a ministry, and the change followed a rebellion that both sides remember as an atrocity committed by the other. A rule of few over many depended on shared administration, and ended when that administration was no longer accepted.
questions: How should the Raj's effects on the economy, famine, and infrastructure be weighed against each other, and by whose standards?
How did Indian institutions and elites shape the Raj rather than only being shaped by it?

event/blling-allerd-warming.title: Bølling-Allerød Warming
event/blling-allerd-warming.summary: The Bølling-Allerød was an abrupt warm interval from about 14,700 to 12,900 years ago, the first major warming after the Last Glacial Maximum. It ended just as abruptly with the onset of the Younger Dryas.
facts: The interval ran from about 14,700 to 12,900 years ago, following the Oldest Dryas, the final cold stage of the retreat from the Last Glacial Maximum.
Warming was abrupt and large in the Northern Hemisphere, while the Southern Hemisphere cooled slightly at the same time, a pattern seen in other rapid climate shifts.
Boreal forest and birch woodland spread across Western Europe and the North European Plain, including Doggerland, replacing tundra vegetation.

A pulse of rapid sea-level rise, Meltwater Pulse 1A, began within the interval as the Laurentide and Eurasian ice sheets lost mass quickly; estimates of the rise range from roughly 10 to 20 meters over a few centuries.
The interval was briefly interrupted by the Older Dryas, a cold spell of one to two centuries whose evidence is strongest in northern Europe, leading some to debate whether it was global or regional.
It ended abruptly with the onset of the Younger Dryas, which itself lasted until about 11,700 years ago, when the Holocene began.
event/blling-allerd-warming.context: The Bølling-Allerød sits within the Pleistocene Epoch, following the Last Glacial Maximum and preceding the Younger Dryas and the Holocene Epoch. See Earth Systems and Life.
event/blling-allerd-warming.observer: The Observer notes that the climate the species inherited did not warm smoothly: a sharp rise, a cold century-long interruption, then a second abrupt swing back to near-glacial cold, all within about three thousand years. The stability that made later farming and cities possible had to wait for the swings to stop. The reading would weaken if closer dating showed the Older Dryas was a purely local signal with no wider significance.
questions: Was the Older Dryas a global cooling event or a regional one?
Which ice sheet contributed most to Meltwater Pulse 1A?

event/cambrian-explosion.title: Cambrian Explosion
event/cambrian-explosion.summary: The Cambrian Explosion is the relatively rapid appearance, over roughly 13 to 25 million years starting 538.8 million years ago, of most major animal body plans in the fossil record.
facts: Animals with hard parts, such as shells and exoskeletons, appear widely.
Famous fossil sites include the Burgess Shale in Canada and Chengjiang in China.
Ediacaran precursors show that animals existed before the Cambrian.
Oxygen levels, ecological arms races, and developmental genetics are all proposed contributors.

event/cambrian-explosion.observer: The Observer sees a burst of experimentation with body design, followed by long conservatism. Innovation clusters, and so does its aftermath.

event/campanian-ignimbrite-eruption.title: Campanian Ignimbrite Eruption
event/campanian-ignimbrite-eruption.summary: The Campanian Ignimbrite eruption of the Campi Flegrei caldera near Naples, Italy, about 39,850 years ago, was the largest explosive eruption in Europe in roughly the last 200,000 years. Its ash spread across the Mediterranean and Eastern Europe, and its role in Neanderthal decline around the same time is debated.
facts: A 2017 study combining radiocarbon and argon dating with a synchronized varve chronology dated the eruption precisely to about 39,850 years ago.
The eruption released roughly 181 to 265 cubic kilometers of magma, a Volcanic Explosivity Index of 7, the largest in Europe in about 200,000 years.
Its ash, the Y-5 layer, dispersed over about 3 million square kilometers and is used as a dated marker in sediment cores from the Mediterranean to the Russian Plain.

The eruption fell close to the onset of Heinrich Event 4, a severe cold phase, but records show the ash postdates that onset by roughly 700 to 800 years, complicating a simple eruption-triggers-cooling account.

Climate modeling found the cooling and acid deposition lasted only one to two years and that the most intense cooling largely missed the Western European areas where late Neanderthal populations lived.

At several Italian sites, modern-human-associated stone tools appear stratigraphically before the ash layer, and some recalibrated Neanderthal extinction dates predate the eruption too; some researchers still argue it shaped cultural change further east, where modeled cooling was stronger.
event/campanian-ignimbrite-eruption.context: The eruption falls within the Paleolithic and is often discussed alongside the Neanderthal Extinction and the decline of Homo neanderthalensis, though a direct link is contested. It occurs near the start of the Upper Paleolithic. See Earth Systems and Life.
event/campanian-ignimbrite-eruption.observer: The Observer treats the pairing of a great eruption with a Neanderthal decline near it in time as an old temptation: a single dramatic cause for a slow disappearance. The dating and modeling done since have mostly weakened that story rather than confirmed it, which the Observer takes as a caution against single-cause explanations for extinctions. The reading would weaken if new modeling showed the strongest cooling did reach the last Neanderthal populations after all.
questions: Did the eruption meaningfully affect Neanderthal populations anywhere, even without its coldest effects in the west?
How exactly does its timing relate to the onset of Heinrich Event 4?

event/carboniferous-coal-forests.title: Carboniferous Coal Forests
event/carboniferous-coal-forests.summary: The Carboniferous coal forests were swamp forests of wet tropical lowlands, mostly in the later Carboniferous, about 323 to 299 million years ago. Their buried plant matter became much of the world's coal.
facts: The forests grew mainly on the lowlands of the northern continent of Euramerica and in parts of China, and included tree-sized club-mosses such as Lepidodendron, tree ferns, giant horsetails and early conifers.
Repeated rises and falls of sea level, linked to the Late Paleozoic Ice Age, drowned and re-exposed the swamps and stacked many separate coal seams.
At Joggins in Nova Scotia, hollow fossil tree stumps contain remains of early amphibians and reptiles.
Burial of plant carbon lowered atmospheric carbon dioxide and probably raised oxygen. Coal from these rocks fuelled the Industrial Revolution in Britain and other regions.
About 305 million years ago the wet tropical forests collapsed into isolated patches as the climate became drier and cooler, an event linked to declines among amphibians and the rise of reptiles.
event/carboniferous-coal-forests.context: The Carboniferous coal forests follow the Devonian Forests and the Rise of Trees and belong to the Carboniferous Period. Their end coincides with the Assembly of Pangaea. The event belongs to the theme thread of Earth Systems and Life.
event/carboniferous-coal-forests.observer: The Observer records the difference in rates: the forests stored their carbon over tens of millions of years, and the species has burned much of it in a few centuries. The reading concerns rates only, and it would not be affected by the debate over why so much coal formed in this period.
questions: Why did so much coal accumulate in this period and not in others?

event/chinese-reform-and-opening.title: Chinese Reform and Opening
event/chinese-reform-and-opening.summary: Beginning in December 1978, China under Deng Xiaoping introduced market reforms and opened to foreign trade, and over the following decades the economy grew rapidly.

Agricultural reforms, the household responsibility system, replaced collective farming in the early 1980s.
Special Economic Zones, including Shenzhen, were established starting in 1980.
China's economy grew at high rates, averaging roughly nine to ten percent a year for several decades.
Hundreds of millions of people were lifted out of extreme poverty.

event/classic-maya-collapse.title: Classic Maya Collapse

No single cause is accepted.

event/closure-of-the-isthmus-of-panama.title: Closure of the Isthmus of Panama
event/closure-of-the-isthmus-of-panama.summary: The Isthmus of Panama, traditionally dated to about 3 million years ago, joined North and South America, closed a sea passage between the Pacific and Atlantic, and triggered a major exchange of land animals.
facts: The land bridge allowed the Great American Biotic Interchange, in which mammals crossed between the continents.
Ground sloths, armadillos, and opossums moved north; cats, dogs, horses, and other groups moved south.
The closure ended the exchange of Pacific and Atlantic waters at low latitudes and is thought to have strengthened Atlantic circulation.
The timing is debated: some studies argue for a much earlier start to the land connection, while others support about 3 million years ago.
Northern glaciation began at about the same time.
event/closure-of-the-isthmus-of-panama.context: The isthmus's closure links ocean circulation, climate, and animal geography in the Cenozoic Era, shortly before the earliest members of the genus Homo such as Homo habilis. Closure of the Isthmus of Panama sits in the Cenozoic Era and the region Planet-wide, and belongs to the theme thread of Earth Systems and Life.
event/closure-of-the-isthmus-of-panama.observer: The Observer notes that a strip of land a few dozen kilometers wide altered the fates of thousands of species on two continents. The same narrow crossing would later matter to humans as a migration route and, much later, as a canal.
questions: When did the land bridge become continuous, and how did that relate to ocean changes?
fact_checks: 2026-09-20: Closure debated between about 2.8 Ma and 13-15 Ma; the Great American Biotic Interchange followed the land bridge [O'Dea et al. 2016 Formation of the Isthmus of Panama]

event/cold-war.title: Cold War
event/cold-war.summary: The Cold War (about 1947 to 1991) was a global rivalry between the United States and the Soviet Union and their allies, fought mainly through arms races, alliances, and proxy wars.
facts: The rivals formed alliances (NATO in 1949, the Warsaw Pact in 1955) and stockpiled nuclear weapons.
The Cuban Missile Crisis of October 1962 is often called the closest approach to nuclear war.
Proxy wars included Korea (1950 to 1953) and Vietnam.
The Berlin Wall stood from 1961 to 1989; the Soviet Union dissolved in December 1991.
event/cold-war.context: The Cold War shaped the Nuclear Age and the Space Age, and influenced Decolonization.
event/cold-war.observer: The Observer notes that two superpowers held the means to destroy each other and did not use them. The restraint is a remarkable feature of the record, and its causes are still debated.
questions: What role did luck play in avoiding nuclear war?

event/collapse-of-the-soviet-union.title: Collapse of the Soviet Union
event/collapse-of-the-soviet-union.summary: The Soviet Union dissolved on 26 December 1991 after the revolutions of 1989 in Eastern Europe and a failed coup in August 1991, ending the Cold War.
facts: The Berlin Wall opened on 9 November 1989.
Mikhail Gorbachev's reforms of glasnost (openness) and perestroika (restructuring) began in the mid-1980s.
Hardliners attempted a coup from 18 to 22 August 1991 and failed.
Russia, Ukraine, and Belarus agreed to dissolve the Union on 8 December 1991.
Fifteen successor states emerged.
event/collapse-of-the-soviet-union.context: The collapse ended the Cold War and the state created by the Russian Revolution seventy years earlier. Collapse of the Soviet Union sits in the Information Age and the region Europe, and belongs to the theme thread of War and Conflict.
event/collapse-of-the-soviet-union.observer: The Observer notes that one of the two largest powers on the planet dissolved with very little fighting between its central institutions. Few observers had predicted this, which suggests that states can be more fragile than their armies imply.
questions: Why was the collapse so widely unforeseen?

event/collision-of-india-and-asia.title: Collision of India and Asia
event/collision-of-india-and-asia.summary: The Indian plate collided with Eurasia beginning about 50 million years ago, raising the Himalaya and the Tibetan Plateau, and the convergence continues today.
facts: India separated from Gondwana and drifted north, unusually fast for a continental plate.
Most estimates place the start of collision at about 50 to 55 million years ago, and the final closure of the Tethys Ocean between about 50 and 60 million years ago.
The collision built the Himalaya, whose highest peak, Mount Everest, is 8,848.86 meters by the 2020 China-Nepal survey.
India still converges on Asia at a few centimeters a year.
The uplift shaped the South Asian monsoon and the sources of the Indus, Ganges, and Brahmaputra rivers.
event/collision-of-india-and-asia.context: The collision produced the mountains and river systems that later shaped South Asia, including the setting of the Indus Valley Civilization. It is a late consequence of the Breakup of Pangaea. Collision of India and Asia sits in the Cenozoic Era and the region South Asia, and belongs to the theme thread of Earth Systems and Life.
event/collision-of-india-and-asia.observer: The Observer notes that the mountains humans treat as fixed boundaries, and the rivers that fed their earliest cities, come from a slow collision still in progress. Geography that looks like destiny is only a snapshot of motion.
questions: When exactly did the first contact occur?
fact_checks: 2026-09-20: Collision began about 50-55 Ma [National Geographic on Everest and Plate Tectonics]

event/colonization-of-land.title: Colonization of Land
event/colonization-of-land.summary: Plants, then arthropods and vertebrates, moved onto land beginning about 470 million years ago, transforming the planet's surface.
facts: The earliest land plant spores are found in Ordovician rocks (about 470 million years old).
Forests appeared in the Devonian, and vast swamp forests in the Carboniferous formed coal.
Early tetrapods evolved from lobe-finned fishes; see Tiktaalik.
Land plants changed soils, rivers, and the carbon cycle.
event/colonization-of-land.context: Colonization of land unfolds through the Paleozoic Era and helped set up the Late Devonian Extinction.
event/colonization-of-land.observer: The Observer notes that Earth's terrestrial life is a late arrival on a planet where life began in water. Coal, the fuel later burned in industrial societies, is a byproduct of this era.
questions: What triggered the move onto land?

event/columbian-exchange.title: Columbian Exchange
event/columbian-exchange.summary: The Columbian Exchange was the transfer of plants, animals, people, and diseases between the Americas and the rest of the world after 1492.
facts: The term was coined by historian Alfred Crosby in 1972.
Old World diseases such as smallpox caused catastrophic mortality among Indigenous peoples of the Americas; estimates of the loss vary widely, from about 50 to 95 percent of the population by 1650.
Maize, potatoes, tomatoes, and cassava spread worldwide, and horses, cattle, and wheat spread to the Americas.
The exchange underpinned the growth of European empires and the Atlantic Slave Trade.
event/columbian-exchange.context: The exchange opens the Early Modern Period and ended a long separation of the two hemispheres. See Aztec Empire, Inca Empire and Mesoamerica.
event/columbian-exchange.observer: The Observer regards this as the moment when the biosphere of the entire planet was mixed at once, an event with no parallel since the continents last joined.
questions: What was the scale of the pre-contact American population?
fact_checks: 2026-09-26: Crosby's 1972 book divided the Columbian Exchange into three categories, diseases, animals and plants; across the Americas populations fell by 50 to 95 percent by 1650; maize (corn), potatoes and cassava spread from the Americas, and wheat, rice and horses to the Americas [Britannica on the Columbian Exchange]

event/congo-free-state.title: Congo Free State
event/congo-free-state.summary: The Congo Free State (1885 to 1908) was a vast territory in Central Africa ruled as the personal possession of King Leopold II of Belgium, notorious for forced labor in rubber and ivory collection and for mass deaths.
facts: The Berlin Conference recognized Leopold's claim to most of the Congo Basin in 1884 to 1885, on the pretext of philanthropy.
Forced labor quotas, hostage-taking, and mutilation were used to force rubber collection.
Estimates of the decline in the Congolese population range from about 1 million to 15 million, with about 10 million the most commonly cited central figure; the numbers are contested.
International outcry led Belgium to take over the colony in 1908.
event/congo-free-state.context: The state was a product of the Scramble for Africa. See Sanctioned Harm and Frontiers of Extraction.
event/congo-free-state.observer: The Observer records this as an extreme case in which a humanitarian story-glue served as cover for extraction. Detachment here does not mean neutrality: the sources are clear about the coercion, and unclear only about the numbers.
questions: How large was the population decline, and how much was due to disease versus violence?
fact_checks: 2026-09-20: Population decline estimates 1 to 15 million, about 10 million most cited; contested [English Wikipedia]

event/control-of-fire.title: Control of Fire
event/control-of-fire.summary: Human ancestors began controlling fire at least around a million years ago, and habitual fire use is well established by about 400,000 years ago.
facts: Evidence at Wonderwerk Cave in South Africa dates to about one million years ago.
Burned seeds, wood, and flint at Gesher Benot Ya'aqov in Israel suggest human control of fire nearly 790,000 years ago.
Earlier claims, at about 1.5 million years, are disputed.
Cooked food is easier to chew and digest, and may have supported larger brains.
event/control-of-fire.context: Fire control is a key event of the Paleolithic associated with Homo erectus. See the essay Fire, Then Everything.
event/control-of-fire.observer: The Observer calls this heat-domestication and treats it as the first true engine the species built: a source of energy outside the body that changed diet, night, and social life.
questions: When did the species learn to make fire, not just use it?
fact_checks: 2026-09-20: Wood ash and burned bone at Wonderwerk Cave about 1 Ma [University of Toronto on Fire at Wonderwerk Cave]

2026-09-26: Burned seeds, wood and flint at the Acheulian site of Gesher Benot Ya'aqov, Israel, are suggestive of human control of fire nearly 790,000 years ago; wood of six taxa was burned [Goren-Inbar et al. 2004 Fire at Gesher Benot Ya'aqov]

event/covid-19-pandemic.title: COVID-19 Pandemic
event/covid-19-pandemic.summary: The COVID-19 pandemic was a global outbreak of the coronavirus SARS-CoV-2, first identified in late 2019.
facts: The World Health Organization declared a pandemic on 11 March 2020 and ended the global health emergency on 5 May 2023.

More than 7 million deaths were officially reported; WHO estimated about 14.9 million excess deaths in 2020 and 2021 (range 13.3 to 16.6 million), nearly three times the reported COVID deaths for that period.
Vaccines using mRNA technology were developed and authorized within about a year.
Lockdowns, remote work, and supply-chain disruption affected economies worldwide.
event/covid-19-pandemic.context: The pandemic followed the pattern of earlier disease spread along trade networks; compare the Black Death. It also relied on the Digital Revolution and on modern Vaccination.
event/covid-19-pandemic.observer: The Observer notes that a virus crossed the planet in weeks along the same exchange-webs that carry goods. It also notes an unusual feature: scientists around the world shared data in real time and produced effective vaccines in a fraction of the historical time.
questions: What were the origins of the virus, and how can future pandemics be prevented?
fact_checks: 2026-09-20: WHO estimate of 14.9 million excess deaths for 2020-2021 (13.3-16.6 million); more than 7 million reported deaths (about 7.1 million by mid-2026) [WHO COVID-19 Mortality Data]

event/cretaceous-paleogene-extinction.title: Cretaceous-Paleogene Extinction
event/cretaceous-paleogene-extinction.summary: The Cretaceous-Paleogene (K-Pg) extinction, about 66 million years ago, wiped out the non-avian dinosaurs and about three-quarters of species after an asteroid struck what is now Mexico.
facts: The Chicxulub impact crater lies beneath the Yucatan Peninsula.
A global layer rich in iridium, an element common in asteroids, was reported by Luis and Walter Alvarez and colleagues in 1980.
Volcanism in the Deccan Traps probably contributed to the stress on ecosystems.
Birds, descended from small feathered dinosaurs, survived; see Dinosaurs.
event/cretaceous-paleogene-extinction.context: The event ends the Mesozoic Era and begins the Cenozoic Era. It gave mammals, including the ancestors of primates, new ecological room.
event/cretaceous-paleogene-extinction.observer: The Observer regards this as the most consequential accident for the species' own story. Human history begins, in a real sense, with a rock falling on Yucatan.
questions: How much did volcanism versus impact matter?
fact_checks: 2026-09-20: Boundary at 66.0 Ma; about 76% of species lost [ICS International Chronostratigraphic Chart; Our World in Data Mass Extinctions]

event/crusades.title: Crusades
event/crusades.summary: The Crusades were a series of religiously sanctioned military expeditions launched by Western European Christians from 1095, largely to capture and hold Jerusalem and other holy sites in the Levant.
facts: Pope Urban II called for the First Crusade at the Council of Clermont in 1095.
The First Crusade captured Jerusalem in 1099 and established Crusader states.
Saladin retook Jerusalem in 1187.
The Fourth Crusade sacked the Christian city of Constantinople in 1204.
The last Crusader stronghold on the mainland, Acre, fell to the Mamluks on 28 May 1291.
event/crusades.context: The Crusades brought Western Europe into sustained contact with the Islamic world and the Byzantine Empire, and involved the sack of Constantinople in 1204. They followed the Rise of Islam and the conquest of the Levant. Crusades sits in the Medieval Period and the region Levant and Anatolia, and belongs to the theme thread of Religion and Belief and War and Conflict.
event/crusades.observer: The Observer notes that a claim-line was fought over for two centuries because both sides considered it sacred. Meaning-engines can turn a piece of ground into something worth dying for in a way no economic calculation would.
questions: How much did the Crusades change trade and knowledge exchange?
fact_checks: 2026-09-27: Pope Urban II proclaimed the First Crusade at the Council of Clermont in November 1095; the First Crusade captured Jerusalem in 1099; Jerusalem surrendered to Saladin after a 12-day siege on 2 October 1187; the Fourth Crusade was diverted to the Byzantine Empire, culminating in the Sack of Constantinople and the Latin Empire of 1204; Qalawun's son Khalil took Acre, the last Crusader mainland stronghold, on 28 May 1291 [Wikipedia on the Crusades]

event/deccan-traps-eruptions.title: Deccan Traps Eruptions
event/deccan-traps-eruptions.summary: The Deccan Traps eruptions were a huge outpouring of lava in west-central India, with the main phases at about 66.3 to 65.5 million years ago. They overlap the end-Cretaceous mass extinction, and their role in it is debated.
facts: The Deccan Traps are among the largest volcanic provinces on Earth; the lava flows pile up to more than two kilometres thick in the Western Ghats and once covered well over a million square kilometres.

Radiometric dating places most of the volume within about a million years around the Cretaceous-Paleogene boundary, with large pulses both before and after the Chicxulub impact. The relative timing is debated.
The eruptions released carbon dioxide and sulfur gases, which could have caused warming, cooling episodes and acid rain, and stressed ecosystems before the impact.
Some recent studies conclude that the impact, not the volcanism, was the main driver of the extinction; the question remains open.
The eruptions are linked to the Réunion hotspot, which India passed over as it drifted north.
event/deccan-traps-eruptions.context: The Deccan Traps Eruptions fall at the end of the Cretaceous Period and overlap the Cretaceous-Paleogene Extinction. They took place before the Collision of India and Asia. The event belongs to the theme thread of Earth Systems and Life.
event/deccan-traps-eruptions.observer: The Observer notes that the end-Cretaceous extinction had at least two candidate causes at nearly the same time, and that separating them depends on dating precision of about a hundred thousand years out of sixty-six million. A single-cause story is easier to tell than to verify. The reading would weaken if dating showed the eruptions ended before the impact.
questions: How much did the eruptions contribute to the extinction relative to the impact?
How did the timing of the biggest lava pulses compare with the impact?

event/decolonization.title: Decolonization
event/decolonization.summary: Decolonization was the process by which most colonies of European empires became independent states, mainly between 1945 and 1975.
facts: The United Nations began with 51 members in 1945 and has 193 today, largely from decolonization.
India and Pakistan became independent in 1947; Ghana, in 1957, was the first sub-Saharan African colony to gain independence; 17 African states became independent in 1960.
Independence was won through both negotiation and war, for example in Algeria (1962).
The Portuguese colonial empire in Africa ended in 1974 to 1975, after the Carnation Revolution of April 1974 overthrew the regime in Lisbon.
event/decolonization.context: Decolonization followed World War II and reshaped Sub-Saharan Africa, South Asia, and Southeast Asia. See Mahatma Gandhi and Nelson Mandela.
event/decolonization.observer: The Observer notes the rapid rewriting of the world's claim-lines: within one generation, most of the planet's land changed from subject to sovereign. Many borders drawn by former empires remain in place.
questions: How did colonial borders shape later conflicts?

event/devonian-forests-and-the-rise-of-t.title: Devonian Forests and the Rise of Trees
event/devonian-forests-and-the-rise-of-t.summary: The Devonian forests were the first forests on Earth, appearing about 385 million years ago and spreading through the rest of the period. Trees evolved independently in several plant lineages, and their roots and litter changed soils, rivers and the carbon cycle.
facts: The Gilboa fossil forest in New York, about 385 million years old, holds some of the oldest known fossil trees, including cladoxylopsids with hollow trunks.
Archaeopteris, a tree with woody trunks and fern-like foliage that grew more than ten metres tall, formed forests across several continents in the Late Devonian.
Trees arose independently in several plant lineages during the Devonian and Carboniferous, including club-mosses, relatives of horsetails and ancestors of seed plants.
Deep roots speeded the chemical weathering of rock and built soils, and atmospheric carbon dioxide fell over the Devonian, which may have contributed to later cooling.
Some researchers link the spread of forests to nutrient runoff and ocean oxygen loss at the time of the Late Devonian Extinction; the link is debated.
event/devonian-forests-and-the-rise-of-t.context: The Devonian forests are a central part of the Colonization of Land and lead into the Carboniferous Coal Forests. They belong to the Devonian Period and the theme thread of Earth Systems and Life.
event/devonian-forests-and-the-rise-of-t.observer: The Observer notes that the tree form was reached by unrelated plant groups, which suggests that some solutions are strongly favoured by the problem, here competition for light, and are not tied to one lineage. The reading would weaken if the different tree forms proved to share a single evolutionary origin.
questions: How large was the effect of forests on Devonian carbon dioxide and climate?

event/digital-revolution.title: Digital Revolution
event/digital-revolution.summary: The Digital Revolution is the spread of digital computing and networks from the mid-20th century on, including the internet (from 1969) and the World Wide Web (from 1989 to 1991).
facts: The first message on ARPANET, a precursor of the internet, was sent in 1969.
Tim Berners-Lee proposed the World Wide Web in 1989 and it became public in 1991.
Smartphones, from about 2007, put networked computers in billions of pockets.
More than five billion people now use the internet.
event/digital-revolution.context: See Digital Computer and Alan Turing. It is the defining process of the Information Age.
event/digital-revolution.observer: The Observer regards this as memory-outsourcing at scale: nearly every human utterance, transaction, and image can now be stored and searched. A record of the species is being written faster than any observer could read.
questions: How will the digital record be preserved and interpreted?

event/divergence-of-the-hominin-lineage.title: Divergence of the Hominin Lineage
event/divergence-of-the-hominin-lineage.summary: The hominin lineage, the line leading to humans, split from the line leading to chimpanzees and bonobos between roughly 6 and 8 million years ago in Africa.
facts: Genetic estimates of the split depend on assumed mutation rates and generation times: one 2006 study placed it no earlier than about 6.3 million years ago, while studies using longer generation times imply earlier dates.
Early candidate hominins include Sahelanthropus tchadensis (about 7 million years ago).
Upright walking (bipedalism) is a key early trait; see Australopithecus afarensis.
A 2006 genetic study proposed that the split was gradual, with interbreeding between the lineages for a time, though this model is disputed.
event/divergence-of-the-hominin-lineage.context: The divergence occurs during the Cenozoic Era and sets the biological stage for Origin of Homo sapiens.
event/divergence-of-the-hominin-lineage.observer: The Observer notes that the species' closest relatives are two other apes. The line between 'them' and 'us' is thinner than most human stories suggest.
questions: Was Sahelanthropus bipedal, and was it a hominin?

event/domestication-of-maize.title: Domestication of Maize
event/domestication-of-maize.summary: Maize (corn) was domesticated from a wild grass called teosinte in southwestern Mexico about 9,000 years ago, and became a staple crop across the Americas.
facts: Genetic studies trace maize to the wild teosinte Zea mays subsp. parviglumis.

Five major morphological differences separate maize from teosinte, and regions throughout the genome contributed to the change. Early maize had tiny cobs; selection over thousands of years produced large ears.
The Maya and Aztecs treated maize as sacred; cooking it with lime (nixtamalization) makes its nutrients available.
Maize is now among the world's most-produced crops by volume.
event/domestication-of-maize.context: Maize was the basis of Mesoamerican states such as the Maya and Aztec Empire. It reached the rest of the world through the Columbian Exchange.
event/domestication-of-maize.observer: The Observer treats this as a second, independent run of the Settling. A grass with a few seeds was reshaped by human selection into a crop that could support cities.
questions: How fast did the crop spread north and south?

event/domestication-of-rice.title: Domestication of Rice
event/domestication-of-rice.summary: Rice (Oryza sativa) was domesticated from wild rice in the Yangtze River region of China beginning around 9,000 to 7,000 years ago, over a long process rather than a single event.
facts: Wild ancestor populations of rice are usually identified as Oryza rufipogon.
Early evidence for rice use and cultivation comes from Yangtze valley sites such as Shangshan, where rice phytoliths date to about 9,000 years ago, and later Kuahuqiao and Hemudu.
Domestication traits such as non-shattering seed heads appeared gradually over thousands of years.
The japonica subspecies is generally traced to the Yangtze region; the indica subspecies is thought to have arisen through later crossing with other rice populations, an origin that is debated.
Rice is a staple for more than half of the world's population.
event/domestication-of-rice.context: Rice was one of the great founder crops of The Agricultural Revolution, alongside wheat and barley in Southwest Asia and maize in Domestication of Maize. Rice paddies became central to East Asian societies. Domestication of Rice sits in the Neolithic and the region East Asia, and belongs to the theme thread of Technology and Kinship and Society.
event/domestication-of-rice.observer: The Observer notes that farming was invented independently on several continents with different plants, yet each time produced denser settlement and stored surplus. The similarity of consequences across different crops is what makes the pattern hard to dismiss as accident.
questions: How many separate domestication events produced modern rice varieties?
fact_checks: 2026-09-26: Japonica rice was domesticated in the Yangtze valley from wild Oryza rufipogon, cultivated there by about 8,000 BP with the key non-shattering trait fixed 1,000 years or more later; indica appears to result from introgression of alleles from japonica [Gross and Zhao 2014 Origins of Domesticated Rice]

event/domestication-of-the-dog.title: Domestication of the Dog
event/domestication-of-the-dog.summary: Dogs descend from a now-extinct population of Pleistocene wolves, but when and where domestication happened is one of the most disputed dates in the whole domestication record. Genetic studies place the split from the nearest known wolf relatives at roughly 40,000 to 20,000 years ago; the oldest widely accepted dog remains, from Bonn-Oberkassel in Germany, are about 14,200 years old.
facts: A 2020 study of 27 ancient dog genomes found all dogs share ancestry distinct from any wolf population sampled today, descending from a single extinct Pleistocene lineage.
The same and related studies place the genetic divergence at roughly 40,000 to 27,000 years ago, with some estimates extending to about 20,000; no tighter date is agreed.

Whether domestication happened once or twice, in separate Eurasian wolf populations that later merged, is argued both ways; a large 2020 study favors a single origin, but other ancient-wolf-genome work has reopened the dual-origin question.
The Bonn-Oberkassel dog, buried with two humans about 14,200 years ago, is one of the first remains universally agreed to be a dog rather than a wolf.

Older candidate "Paleolithic dogs" from Goyet Cave, Belgium, and Předmostí, Czech Republic, roughly 30,000 years or more, remain disputed: their skulls do not clearly exclude wolves, and one Předmostí specimen is genetically closer to wolves.
Evidence points to an origin somewhere in Eurasia, often argued to be Siberia, though the region is unsettled.
event/domestication-of-the-dog.context: Dog domestication falls within the Paleolithic, likely spanning the Upper Paleolithic, and is tied to Homo sapiens hunter-gatherer groups. It is the earliest known domestication of any animal, well before plants and livestock. See Kinship and Society and Technology.
event/domestication-of-the-dog.observer: The Observer notes that the species' oldest tool-lineage partnership was with another animal, formed while both still hunted large Ice Age prey, long before writing or farming. The wide, unsettled range of dates, and the difficulty of telling an early dog from a wolf by bone shape alone, means the Observer treats any specific date here as provisional. The reading would weaken if an uncontested dog skeleton were found well outside the 40,000-to-14,000-year range.
questions: Did domestication happen once or more than once?
Which disputed "Paleolithic dog" specimens are true dogs rather than wolves?

event/dutch-east-india-company.title: Dutch East India Company
event/dutch-east-india-company.summary: The Dutch East India Company (VOC) was a chartered trading company founded in 1602 with a monopoly on Dutch trade in Asia, among the first companies to issue tradable shares.
facts: The Dutch States General chartered it in 1602.
It sold shares that were traded on the Amsterdam exchange and is often described as one of the first publicly traded companies.
It had powers to wage war, build forts, and make treaties in Asia.
It founded Batavia (now Jakarta) in 1619.
In 1621 its forces killed or expelled most of the population of the Banda Islands to secure a monopoly on nutmeg; it was dissolved in 1799.
event/dutch-east-india-company.context: The company built on the sea route opened by the Portuguese Sea Route to India and competed in the Indian Ocean Trade Network. It also transported enslaved people and took part in the wider Atlantic Slave Trade system. Dutch East India Company sits in the Early Modern Period and the region Southeast Asia, and belongs to the theme thread of Trade and Economy and War and Conflict.
event/dutch-east-india-company.observer: The Observer notes that a joint-stock company could raise fleets, fight wars, and rule territory, while being owned by strangers who held paper shares. It is a story-glue entity with more sovereignty than most kings.
questions: How central was violence to the company's commercial success?

event/earliest-continental-crust.title: Earliest Continental Crust
event/earliest-continental-crust.summary: The earliest continental crust is the first granite-like crust, lighter than the ocean floor, that could stand above sea level. It may have formed before 4.0 billion years ago, but almost none of it survives as rock, so its extent and timing are uncertain.
facts: Some researchers read the chemistry of Jack Hills zircons, up to about 4.4 billion years old, as showing granite-like magmas, a sign of evolved crust; others dispute that reading. See Jack Hills Zircons.

The Acasta Gneiss in northwestern Canada, about 4.0 billion years old, is the oldest known intact rock body. Some studies date rocks of the Nuvvuagittuq belt in Quebec to as much as about 4.3 billion years, but that age is disputed.
Continental crust is less dense than oceanic crust and is made by partial melting of older rocks. Because it is buoyant it survives recycling far better than the ocean floor.
How fast the continents grew is debated: some models place most of the crust in existence by about 3 billion years ago, and others favour slower growth.
event/earliest-continental-crust.context: The earliest continental crust belongs to the Hadean Eon and continues into the Archean Eon, when the first stable continental cores formed. It is tied to the Formation of the Oceans and to the question of the Onset of Plate Tectonics. The event belongs to the theme thread of Earth Systems and Life.
event/earliest-continental-crust.observer: The Observer notes that the earliest crust is known almost entirely from grains that survived billions of years of recycling. The first half billion years of the record is thin by nature, and the absence of rock is not evidence of the absence of crust. The reading would weaken if new discoveries of ancient rock gave a very different picture.
questions: How much continental crust existed in the Hadean?
Are the oldest claimed rock ages, such as those from Nuvvuagittuq, reliable?
