event/early-hominin-dispersals-from-afri.title: Early Hominin Dispersals from Africa
event/early-hominin-dispersals-from-afri.summary: Hominins first left Africa between about 2.1 and 1.8 million years ago and spread across Eurasia in several dispersals over the next million years. The oldest hominin fossils outside Africa, at Dmanisi in Georgia, are about 1.85 to 1.78 million years old, and stone tools from the Loess Plateau of China are about 2.1 million years old.
facts: Dmanisi has yielded five well-preserved skulls and many body bones, dated to about 1.85 to 1.77 million years ago, with simple Oldowan-style stone tools.
The skulls have small brains, about 546 to 775 cubic centimeters. A 2013 study argued that their variation fits one population, which doubts separate early Homo species.
Stone tools at Shangchen on the Chinese Loess Plateau date from about 2.1 to 1.3 million years ago. No hominin fossils were found there, so the toolmakers are unidentified.
Homo erectus was on Java by about 1.5 to 1.3 million years ago, and hominins were in Spain by about 1.4 to 1.2 million years ago and in England about 0.9 million years ago.
Whether the first dispersers were Homo erectus is debated; small brains and simple tools at Dmanisi suggest they left before that form was typical.
event/early-hominin-dispersals-from-afri.context: The early dispersals follow the Emergence of the Genus Homo and the Oldowan Stone Tools and belong to the Lower Paleolithic. They center on Homo erectus. Homo floresiensis on Flores may descend from an early dispersal; its ancestry is debated. Later dispersals are separate; see Out of Africa Dispersal. See Earth Systems and Life and Technology.
event/early-hominin-dispersals-from-afri.observer: The Observer notes that the first hominins outside Africa had small brains and simple stone tools, which suggests that leaving Africa did not require the large brain of later humans. The Observer reads dispersal as repeated range expansion into new habitats, of which the species' later spread is one more instance. The reading would weaken if the Dmanisi hominins proved an isolated dead end.
questions: Who made the 2.1-million-year-old stone tools at Shangchen?
Did the first hominins to leave Africa belong to Homo erectus or to an earlier form?

event/emergence-of-symbolic-art.title: Emergence of Symbolic Art
event/emergence-of-symbolic-art.summary: Symbolic behavior, including engraved ochre, beads, and cave paintings, appears in the archaeological record from about 100,000 years ago onward.
facts: Engraved ochre from Blombos Cave in South Africa dates to about 75,000 to 100,000 years ago.
Cave paintings in Sulawesi, Indonesia, include a warty-pig painting at least 45,500 years old, and narrative scenes reported in 2024 to be at least 51,200 years old.
European sites such as Chauvet and Lascaux date to about 36,000 and 17,000 years ago.
Some evidence suggests that Neanderthals also made symbolic objects, though this is debated.
event/emergence-of-symbolic-art.context: Symbolic art belongs to the Paleolithic and probably relates to the spread of language and belief; see Language and Writing and Art and Ritual.
event/emergence-of-symbolic-art.observer: The Observer treats this as the first clear sign of a species that lives partly in imagined worlds. A painted animal on a wall implies a viewer who understands that a picture can stand for something absent.
questions: Was the origin of symbolic behavior gradual or sudden?

event/emergence-of-the-genus-homo.title: Emergence of the Genus Homo
event/emergence-of-the-genus-homo.summary: The genus Homo emerged in East Africa between about 2.8 and 1.8 million years ago from an Australopithecus-like ancestor. The oldest fossil assigned to Homo is a partial jaw from Ledi-Geraru, Ethiopia, about 2.8 million years old, but fossils from this interval are sparse and disputed.
facts: The Ledi-Geraru jaw, LD 350-1, is dated to about 2.80 to 2.75 million years ago and was assigned to Homo in 2015. Some later analyses stress its resemblance to Australopithecus afarensis.

A maxilla from Hadar, Ethiopia, about 2.3 million years old, and fossils attributed to Homo habilis and Homo rudolfensis from Olduvai Gorge and Lake Turkana, roughly 2.4 to 1.4 million years old, are assigned to Homo by many researchers. Some place the latter two outside the genus.
Homo erectus appears about 1.9 to 1.8 million years ago with a larger body and brain; see Homo erectus.

Oldowan tools appear about 2.6 million years ago, and older tools from Lomekwi, Kenya, are about 3.3 million years old. Australopithecus and early Homo overlapped, so the earliest toolmaker is uncertain.
East African climate grew drier and more variable across this interval; a link to the origin of Homo is debated.
event/emergence-of-the-genus-homo.context: Homo emerges after Australopithecus afarensis and the Divergence of the Hominin Lineage, during the Onset of Northern Hemisphere Glaciation. It runs through the early Lower Paleolithic with the Oldowan Stone Tools and Homo habilis, and leads to the Early Hominin Dispersals from Africa. See Earth Systems and Life and Technology.
event/emergence-of-the-genus-homo.observer: The Observer notes that the species' own genus has no clean starting line: a jaw at 2.8 million years, scattered skulls near 2 million, and a well-defined body plan only by 1.9 million. The Observer reads this as slow, patchy change in a lineage already walking upright, with no single moment to call a beginning. The reading would weaken if a well-dated skeleton showed a rapid change.
questions: Is the Ledi-Geraru jaw an early Homo or a late Australopithecus?
Which hominin made the first stone tools?

event/enlightenment.title: Enlightenment
event/enlightenment.summary: The Enlightenment was an 18th-century intellectual movement in Europe that emphasized reason, evidence, and individual rights, and challenged traditional authority.
facts: Key figures include John Locke, Voltaire, Montesquieu, Jean-Jacques Rousseau, and Immanuel Kant.
The Encyclopedie, edited by Denis Diderot and Jean d'Alembert, was published between 1751 and 1772.
Adam Smith published The Wealth of Nations in 1776.
Its ideas circulated in salons, coffeehouses, and journals.

Enlightenment thinkers held divergent views on slavery and colonialism: many, including Diderot and Kant, criticized them, while some contributed to racial classifications that were used to justify them.
event/enlightenment.context: The Enlightenment built on the Scientific Revolution, especially the work of Isaac Newton, and supplied ideas for the Age of Revolutions. Enlightenment sits in the Early Modern Period and the region Europe, and belongs to the theme thread of Science and Religion and Belief.
event/enlightenment.observer: The Observer notes that a movement that placed reason above tradition became a tradition itself, with founders and sacred texts. Even critics of meaning-engines end up building one.
questions: How consistent were Enlightenment principles with the practice of empire?

event/eocene-oligocene-transition.title: Eocene-Oligocene Transition
event/eocene-oligocene-transition.summary: The Eocene-Oligocene transition was a sharp global cooling about 34 million years ago, during which permanent ice sheets grew on Antarctica. It marks the shift from a warm greenhouse world toward the colder world of the later Cenozoic.
facts: The boundary between the Eocene and the Oligocene is dated to about 33.9 million years ago. Ocean records show a stepwise rise in oxygen isotopes, read as the combined effect of cooling and the growth of ice.
The Antarctic ice sheet grew to a size close to that of today within a few hundred thousand years, and sea level fell by tens of metres.

Falling atmospheric carbon dioxide, crossing a threshold, is a leading explanation. The opening of ocean gateways around Antarctica, including the Drake Passage and the Tasmanian Gateway, allowed a circumpolar current that isolated the continent; the timing of the openings, between about 50 and 30 million years ago, is debated.
In Europe the change coincides with the Grande Coupure, a turnover in which Asian mammals largely replaced the older European fauna. Marine plankton also suffered extinctions.
event/eocene-oligocene-transition.context: The Eocene-Oligocene Transition follows the warmth of the Paleocene-Eocene Thermal Maximum in the Paleogene Period and prepares the way for the Onset of Northern Hemisphere Glaciation. The event belongs to the theme thread of Earth Systems and Life.
event/eocene-oligocene-transition.observer: The Observer notes that the change looks like a threshold: a slow decline in carbon dioxide produced a rapid reorganisation once a critical level was crossed. The Observer files threshold behaviour as a feature of the climate system that the record shows plainly and that is hard to forecast in detail. The reading would weaken if the ice growth proved gradual, tracking carbon dioxide smoothly.
questions: Was falling carbon dioxide or the opening of Southern Ocean gateways the main cause?
How quickly did the ice sheet reach its full size?

event/fall-of-constantinople.title: Fall of Constantinople
event/fall-of-constantinople.summary: On 29 May 1453, Ottoman forces under Sultan Mehmed II captured Constantinople after a siege of about eight weeks, ending the Byzantine Empire.
facts: The siege lasted from 6 April to 29 May 1453.
The last Byzantine emperor, Constantine XI, died in the final assault.
The Ottomans used very large cannon, including those cast by the Hungarian engineer Urban (also spelled Orban).
The city became the Ottoman capital, later called Istanbul.
Byzantine scholars who moved to Italy are often said to have contributed to Renaissance learning, though the extent is debated.
event/fall-of-constantinople.context: The fall ended the Byzantine Empire, a state that had continued the Roman Empire in the east, and transformed Constantinople into the capital of the Ottoman Empire. The event showed the power of Gunpowder artillery against old walls. Fall of Constantinople sits in the Medieval Period and the region Levant and Anatolia, and belongs to the theme thread of War and Conflict and Religion and Belief.
event/fall-of-constantinople.observer: The Observer notes that a city protected by walls for a thousand years fell to a new technology within weeks. Structures built for one era's weapons offer no security in the next.
questions: How much did the fall affect European trade routes?

event/fall-of-the-western-roman-empire.title: Fall of the Western Roman Empire
event/fall-of-the-western-roman-empire.summary: The Western Roman Empire ended in 476 CE, when the Germanic general Odoacer deposed the last western emperor, Romulus Augustulus.
facts: The 'fall' was a long process, marked by events such as the sack of Rome by the Visigoths in 410.
The Eastern Roman (Byzantine) Empire continued until 1453.
Political authority in the west passed to successor kingdoms.
Historians debate whether it was a collapse or a transformation.
event/fall-of-the-western-roman-empire.context: See Romans, Rome, and Constantinople. The event ends Classical Antiquity in the west and begins the Medieval Period.

event/first-fleet-and-the-colonization-o.title: First Fleet and the Colonization of Australia
event/first-fleet-and-the-colonization-o.summary: The First Fleet of eleven British ships reached Botany Bay in January 1788 carrying about 1,400 people, roughly half of them convicts, and founded the colony of New South Wales at Sydney Cove.
facts: The fleet arrived at Botany Bay on 18 to 20 January 1788 and settled at Sydney Cove on 26 January.
Aboriginal Australians had lived on the continent for at least 50,000 years, and before 1788 they spoke more than 250 languages.
The British claimed the land under the legal doctrine of terra nullius, which was rejected by the High Court of Australia in the Mabo decision of 3 June 1992.
A smallpox epidemic struck Aboriginal communities around Sydney in 1789.
Colonization led to conflict, dispossession, and population decline among Aboriginal peoples.
event/first-fleet-and-the-colonization-o.context: The fleet established a colony on land occupied for tens of thousands of years by Aboriginal Australians, descendants of the Peopling of Sahul. It contrasts with the Treaty of Waitangi signed in New Zealand in 1840. First Fleet and the Colonization of Australia sits in the Industrial Age and the region Oceania, and belongs to the theme thread of War and Conflict and Kinship and Society.
event/first-fleet-and-the-colonization-o.observer: The Observer notes that the same species held two conflicting claim-lines over the same land: one built on tens of millennia of use, the other on a legal fiction that no one owned it. Which claim prevailed was decided by weapons and disease, and later revised by courts.
questions: What was the Aboriginal population in 1788?

event/fish-to-tetrapod-transition.title: Fish-to-Tetrapod Transition
event/fish-to-tetrapod-transition.summary: The Fish-to-Tetrapod Transition was the evolution of four-limbed vertebrates from lobe-finned fishes in the Middle and Late Devonian, roughly 385 to 360 million years ago. The sequence is well documented, but its start is debated.
facts: Tetrapods descend from lobe-finned fishes, a group whose fins hold a central skeleton of bones.

Transitional fossils include Panderichthys from Latvia, about 380 million years old, Tiktaalik from the Canadian Arctic, about 375 million years old, and Acanthostega and Ichthyostega from Greenland, about 365 million years old. The last two had limbs with digits but lived mostly in water.
Limbs probably evolved for moving through shallow, vegetated water, and were used on land later; that reading is a hypothesis.

Trackways from Zachełmie in Poland, dated to about 395 million years ago, have been read as tetrapod footprints. That would place limbed animals earlier than the known body fossils, but the interpretation is debated.
event/fish-to-tetrapod-transition.context: The Fish-to-Tetrapod Transition falls in the Devonian Period and is one thread of the Colonization of Land. It precedes the Late Devonian Extinction. The event belongs to the theme threads of Earth Systems and Life and Science.
event/fish-to-tetrapod-transition.observer: The Observer notes that the transition shows a feature's later use need not match its origin: limbs seem to have arisen for water and been used on land afterwards. It also notes that the fossils were found in part by predicting the rock age and setting where they should occur, which is an unusually testable case for the record. The reading would weaken if the earliest limbs proved to have served mainly for walking on land.
questions: How old is the origin of limbed tetrapods, given the Zachełmie trackways?
Which living fish groups, if any, preserve traits of the first limbed animals?

event/formation-of-the-oceans.title: Formation of the Oceans
event/formation-of-the-oceans.summary: The Formation of the Oceans is the time, probably between about 4.4 and 4.0 billion years ago, when liquid water first collected on Earth's surface as the young planet cooled. The date is uncertain and rests on indirect evidence.
facts: Oxygen-isotope ratios in some Jack Hills zircons, dated to about 4.4 billion years ago, have been read as evidence that their parent magma had interacted with liquid water; that reading is contested. See Jack Hills Zircons.

Earth's water came from the material that built the planet and from later impacts of water-rich bodies. Asteroids of the carbonaceous chondrite type match the hydrogen isotopes of ocean water well, but the shares from each source are debated.
The young Sun gave only about 70 percent of its present light, so liquid water at the surface needed a strong greenhouse effect from gases such as carbon dioxide.
The oldest rocks that clearly formed in water, including sediments and pillow-shaped lavas at Isua in Greenland, are about 3.7 to 3.8 billion years old, so oceans existed by then.
The depth of the early oceans and the amount of land above them are debated.
event/formation-of-the-oceans.context: The Formation of the Oceans falls in the Hadean Eon, after the Theia Impact and the Formation of the Moon and around the Late Heavy Bombardment. The oceans were the setting for the Origin of Life. The event belongs to the theme thread of Earth Systems and Life.
event/formation-of-the-oceans.observer: The Observer files the oceans under preconditions: every later subject in the record assumes liquid water. That the planet had it depended on its size, its distance from the Sun and the contingent delivery of water, and the Observer treats the outcome as favourable circumstance, not design. The reading would weaken if water proved a near-inevitable product of planet formation at this distance.
questions: How much of Earth's water was present at formation and how much arrived later?

event/formation-of-the-solar-system-and-.title: Formation of the Solar System and Earth
event/formation-of-the-solar-system-and-.summary: The Solar System formed about 4.57 billion years ago from a collapsing cloud of gas and dust, and Earth accreted from that material over tens of millions of years.
facts: The Sun formed at the center of the collapsing cloud, and a disk of material around it clumped into planets.
The oldest dated solids in the Solar System are calcium-aluminum-rich inclusions in meteorites, about 4.567 billion years old.
Earth's age of about 4.54 billion years comes from radiometric dating of meteorites and of Earth's oldest lead.
Earth's early interior heated and separated into a metallic core and rocky mantle.
event/formation-of-the-solar-system-and-.context: Earth's formation begins the Hadean Eon. The Moon-forming impact, Theia Impact and the Formation of the Moon, followed shortly after.
event/formation-of-the-solar-system-and-.observer: The Observer notes that every atom heavier than helium in the species' bodies was made in earlier stars. The 'birth' of Earth is a rearrangement of old material, not a beginning from nothing.
questions: How quickly did Earth's core form?

event/french-revolution.title: French Revolution
event/french-revolution.summary: The French Revolution (1789 to 1799) overthrew the monarchy in France, declared the rights of man and citizen, and led to the rise of Napoleon Bonaparte.
facts: The storming of the Bastille took place on 14 July 1789.
The Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen was adopted in August 1789.
Louis XVI was executed in January 1793, and the Reign of Terror followed in 1793 and 1794, killing tens of thousands.
The revolutionary government introduced the metric system.
Napoleon seized power in a coup in 1799.
event/french-revolution.context: The revolution drew on ideas of the Enlightenment and was a central event of the Age of Revolutions. It spread to the colonies and inspired the Haitian Revolution. French Revolution sits in the Industrial Age and the region Europe, and belongs to the theme thread of War and Conflict and Kinship and Society.
event/french-revolution.observer: The Observer notes that a revolution that began by declaring universal rights ended by executing many of its own leaders. Movements that claim to represent everyone find it hard to accommodate disagreement.
questions: How far did the revolution continue the centralizing policies of the monarchy?

event/genomic-revolution.title: Genomic Revolution
event/genomic-revolution.summary: The Genomic Revolution began with the identification of the DNA double helix in 1953 and has made it possible to read and edit the genetic code of living things.
facts: James Watson and Francis Crick proposed the double-helix structure in 1953, using X-ray data from Rosalind Franklin and Maurice Wilkins.
The Human Genome Project ran from 1990 to 2003; the first complete, gap-free sequence of a human genome (all chromosomes except Y) was published in 2022.
CRISPR gene editing was developed in 2012.
Ancient DNA has transformed prehistory, including the sequencing of the Homo neanderthalensis genome in 2010 and the discovery of Denisovans.
event/genomic-revolution.context: The revolution depends on the Digital Revolution for computing power and reshaped medicine and our understanding of human origins.
event/genomic-revolution.observer: The Observer notes that the species has learned to read the instructions from which it is built, and to change them. It also can read the DNA of long-dead relatives.
questions: What limits should govern editing the human genome?

event/great-acceleration.title: Great Acceleration
event/great-acceleration.summary: The Great Acceleration is the sharp, simultaneous rise since about 1950 in human population, energy use, economic output, and environmental change.
facts: The term was used by the International Geosphere-Biosphere Programme; a 2015 study charted 24 indicators.
Global population rose from about 2.5 billion in 1950 to about 8 billion in 2022.
Energy use, fertilizer use, and greenhouse gas emissions rose steeply.
Many Earth-system indicators (extinction rates, ocean acidity, carbon dioxide) changed in parallel.
event/great-acceleration.context: The Great Acceleration is a main candidate for the start of the Anthropocene. See The Species as a Geological Force and Modern Climate Change.
event/great-acceleration.observer: The Observer treats 1950 as a hinge: curves for population, energy, and impact all bend upward at once. The scale of change within a single human lifetime has no earlier parallel.
questions: Which of the curves can be bent, and how quickly?

event/great-ordovician-biodiversificatio.title: Great Ordovician Biodiversification
event/great-ordovician-biodiversificatio.summary: The Great Ordovician Biodiversification was a long rise in the diversity of marine animals, running from about 485 to 460 million years ago. It multiplied the number of species and families within body plans that had first appeared in the Cambrian.
facts: By some counts, marine diversity at the family and genus level rose several-fold between the Early and Middle Ordovician.
Brachiopods, bryozoans, molluscs, echinoderms such as crinoids, corals and sponges all diversified, and reefs and filter-feeding communities grew more complex. Plankton diversified as well.
The Cambrian Explosion produced the body plans; the Ordovician diversification filled out the variety within them.
Proposed causes include a cooling from the hot Cambrian climate, more oxygen, nutrients from volcanism, more shallow shelf habitat and ecological feedbacks. The mix is debated.
The rise ended near the close of the period with the Late Ordovician Extinction.
event/great-ordovician-biodiversificatio.context: The Great Ordovician Biodiversification is the main event of the Ordovician Period within the Paleozoic Era and follows the Cambrian Explosion. The event belongs to the theme threads of Earth Systems and Life and Science.
event/great-ordovician-biodiversificatio.observer: The Observer notes that variety depends on ecological space as well as on novelty: the same body plans, given new habitats and richer food webs, yielded far more forms. It reads the event as a slow build after a fast start. The reading would weaken if diversity had risen with no link to habitat or climate.
questions: What drove the biodiversification: climate, ocean chemistry, ecology, or a combination?
How much of the apparent rise reflects better preservation of Ordovician rocks?

event/great-oxidation-event.title: Great Oxidation Event
event/great-oxidation-event.summary: The Great Oxidation Event was the rise of free oxygen in Earth's atmosphere beginning about 2.4 billion years ago, driven by photosynthetic microbes.
facts: Oxygen-producing photosynthesis by Cyanobacteria gradually saturated chemical sinks such as dissolved iron.
Banded iron formations record the process in rock.
Oxygen was poisonous to much anaerobic life; some scientists infer a major biological turnover.
It may be linked to the Huronian glaciation, one of the earliest ice ages.
event/great-oxidation-event.context: The event opens the Proterozoic Eon. Oxygen later supported complex life, including animals; see Cambrian Explosion.
event/great-oxidation-event.observer: The Observer notes a lesson that recurs in the record: a living population can change the planet so much that it reshapes its own future. The species is the second case, not the first.
questions: How long did the transition take?
fact_checks: 2026-09-20: GOE began about 2.46-2.43 Ga and ended about 2.06 Ga; cyanobacterial oxygen first oxidized dissolved iron; Huronian glaciation began about 2.4 Ga [Wikipedia on the Great Oxidation Event]

event/green-revolution.title: Green Revolution
event/green-revolution.summary: The Green Revolution was the spread of high-yield crop varieties, fertilizers, and irrigation from the 1940s to the 1970s, which greatly increased grain production.
facts: Plant breeder Norman Borlaug developed high-yield semi-dwarf wheat in Mexico, and IR8 rice was released in 1966.
India, Pakistan, Mexico, and the Philippines were among the earliest and largest adopters.
The revolution is credited with averting large famines, but also brought heavy fertilizer and water use.
Yields and populations rose together.
event/green-revolution.context: The Green Revolution fed the growth of the Great Acceleration. Compare it with The Agricultural Revolution.
event/green-revolution.observer: The Observer sees a second Settling: another jump in food that let the species grow by billions. The Haber-Bosch process, which fixes nitrogen for fertilizer, now supports a large share of the species' food supply.
questions: What were the long-term ecological costs?

event/haitian-revolution.title: Haitian Revolution
event/haitian-revolution.summary: The Haitian Revolution (1791 to 1804) was a rebellion of enslaved people against the French colony of Saint-Domingue that created the independent state of Haiti.
facts: Saint-Domingue was one of the most profitable sugar colonies in the world.
An uprising began in August 1791; Toussaint Louverture became its most prominent leader.
Independence was declared on 1 January 1804, making Haiti the first republic founded by formerly enslaved people.
France later demanded a large indemnity (1825), which burdened Haiti's economy for generations.
event/haitian-revolution.context: The revolution is a central event of the Age of Revolutions and a turning point in the history of the Atlantic Slave Trade.
event/haitian-revolution.observer: The Observer notes that the language of universal rights, which the revolutionaries of France also used, was taken at its word by people the authors had excluded. Story-glue can be turned against those who wrote it.
questions: How did the indemnity shape Haiti's later development?

event/holocaust.title: Holocaust
event/holocaust.summary: The Holocaust was the persecution of European Jews by Nazi Germany from 1933 and the systematic murder of about six million of them from 1941 to 1945, with the help of allies and collaborators.
facts: Persecution began after the Nazi rise to power in 1933 and included exclusion, expropriation, and the Nuremberg Laws of 1935.
Systematic mass murder began in 1941, first by shootings in the occupied Soviet Union, then in extermination camps such as Auschwitz-Birkenau, Treblinka, and Sobibor.
About six million Jews were killed.
The Nazis also murdered Roma and Sinti, disabled people, Soviet prisoners of war, and political opponents.
The word genocide was coined by Raphael Lemkin in 1944, and the UN adopted the Genocide Convention in 1948.
event/holocaust.context: The Holocaust took place within World War II and is the most thoroughly documented case of Sanctioned Harm by a modern state. Holocaust sits in the Industrial Age and the region Europe, and belongs to the theme thread of War and Conflict and Kinship and Society.
event/holocaust.observer: The Observer records this as an atrocity carried out by an industrial, literate, bureaucratic society, and declines to explain it away. The evidence shows that ordinary institutions, records, and technologies were used for extermination, which is why the species keeps returning to the question of how this occurred.
questions: How did ordinary people come to take part?

event/huronian-glaciation.title: Huronian Glaciation
event/huronian-glaciation.summary: The Huronian glaciation was a series of ice ages recorded in the Huronian Supergroup of Ontario, Canada, in the early Paleoproterozoic, about 2.4 to 2.2 billion years ago. It is one of the oldest well-documented ice ages.
facts: The Huronian Supergroup, north of Lake Huron, contains three glacial deposits, the Ramsay Lake, Bruce and Gowganda formations, separated by sediments laid down in warmer conditions.

Glacial deposits of similar age are reported from other continents, including Wyoming and Finland. The Makganyene Formation in South Africa, about 2.2 billion years old, formed near the equator, which supports an early snowball state, though its link to the Huronian is debated.

The glaciation follows the first rise of oxygen. One hypothesis is that oxygen destroyed atmospheric methane, a strong greenhouse gas, and so cooled the planet; other explanations involve volcanic and tectonic change.
How long the ice lasted, and whether it covered the whole planet, are debated.
event/huronian-glaciation.context: The Huronian Glaciation falls in the Paleoproterozoic Era soon after the Great Oxidation Event began, and it is the earliest of the ice ages of the Proterozoic Eon before Snowball Earth. The event belongs to the theme thread of Earth Systems and Life.
event/huronian-glaciation.observer: The Observer files the Huronian under a caution about attribution: an ice age and an oxygen rise that share a date invite a causal story, and the story is plausible, but the record allows other explanations. The reading would strengthen or weaken with tighter dating of the glacial deposits against the first traces of oxygen.
questions: Did the oxygen rise cause the glaciation, or did the two arise from a common cause?
Was the ice global?

event/incense-trade.title: Incense Trade
event/incense-trade.summary: The incense trade carried frankincense and myrrh from southern Arabia and the Horn of Africa to Mediterranean and Mesopotamian markets, mostly by camel caravan, for well over a thousand years.
facts: Frankincense comes from Boswellia trees growing in southern Arabia, including Oman and Yemen, and in the Horn of Africa.
Incense was burned in temples and at funerals across the Egyptian, Greek, and Roman worlds.
Caravans traveled northward through western Arabia to the Levant.
Kingdoms such as Saba and the Nabataeans profited from taxing and guiding the caravans.
The trade declined in the later Roman period, with reduced demand often cited as one cause.
event/incense-trade.context: The trade linked the Arabian Peninsula to the Mediterranean Basin and predates the broader Opening of the Silk Roads. It supported the wealth of Kingdom of Saba and the Nabataeans. Incense Trade sits in the Iron Age and the region Arabian Peninsula, and belongs to the theme thread of Trade and Economy and Religion and Belief.
event/incense-trade.observer: The Observer notes that an aromatic resin, burned to nothing, sustained kingdoms in desert country for centuries. Demand for a substance with no material use shows how much of exchange is driven by ritual rather than survival.
questions: How much did the route change with the domestication of the camel?

event/indian-ocean-trade-network.title: Indian Ocean Trade Network
event/indian-ocean-trade-network.summary: The Indian Ocean trade network was a system of sea routes linking East Africa, Arabia, South Asia, Southeast Asia, and China, and it was busiest from about the 8th to the 15th century CE.
facts: Seasonal monsoon winds allowed ships to sail east in one season and return in another.
Traded goods included spices, cotton textiles, ivory, gold, and Chinese porcelain.
Swahili city-states such as Kilwa on the East African coast grew rich on it; see Swahili Coast City-States.
Portuguese ships entered the ocean in 1498 and began to seize control of key ports.
event/indian-ocean-trade-network.context: The network complemented the overland Opening of the Silk Roads and carried Islam and other religions along its ports. See Zheng He.
event/indian-ocean-trade-network.observer: The Observer notes that the wind itself acted as a scheduler. A predictable natural cycle allowed strangers of many faiths to run a shared exchange-web for centuries with little central authority.
questions: How large was the volume of trade compared to overland routes?

event/indian-rebellion-of-1857.title: Indian Rebellion of 1857
event/indian-rebellion-of-1857.summary: The Indian Rebellion of 1857 began as a mutiny of sepoys (Indian soldiers) of the East India Company army at Meerut on 10 May 1857 and grew into a wider uprising across northern and central India, ending British East India Company rule.
facts: The rebellion lasted until 1858 and was suppressed by the British.
The rebel leaders included the last Mughal emperor and Rani Lakshmibai of Jhansi, who died in battle on 17 June 1858.
A Royal Proclamation of 1 November 1858 transferred rule from the Company to the British Crown.
It is called the Sepoy Mutiny by many British writers and the First War of Independence by many Indian historians.

event/indian-removal-and-the-trail-of-te.title: Indian Removal and the Trail of Tears
event/indian-removal-and-the-trail-of-te.summary: The Indian Removal Act of 1830 authorized the United States to relocate Native American nations from the southeastern states to lands west of the Mississippi, leading to forced marches known as the Trail of Tears.
facts: The Act was signed by President Andrew Jackson in 1830.
It affected the Cherokee, Choctaw, Chickasaw, Creek, and Seminole nations.
In 1838 to 1839, about 16,000 Cherokee were forced to march west; commonly cited estimates put deaths at around 4,000.
The Supreme Court had ruled in Worcester v. Georgia (1832) in favor of Cherokee rights, but the ruling was not enforced.
event/indian-removal-and-the-trail-of-te.context: The removals were part of the westward expansion of the United States in North America. Compare the political traditions of the Haudenosaunee Confederacy.
event/indian-removal-and-the-trail-of-te.observer: The Observer notes that a legal system ruled in favor of a people, and the executive branch declined to enforce it. Law is only one part of what determines outcomes; enforcement is another.
questions: What were the total deaths across all the removals?

event/indo-european-language-spread.title: Indo-European Language Spread
event/indo-european-language-spread.summary: Languages of the Indo-European family, including ancestors of English, Hindi, Persian, Greek, Latin, and Russian, spread across Eurasia beginning several thousand years ago. Where the family began is still disputed.
facts: Today, Indo-European languages are the first language of roughly 40 to 46 percent of the world's population, depending on the estimate.

The leading view for the Indo-European homeland has been the Pontic-Caspian steppe, supported by ancient DNA from Yamnaya-related groups. Two papers in Nature in 2025 refine this. They place the ancestral community, speaking what they call proto-Indo-Anatolian, in the Caucasus-Lower Volga region about 4400 to 4000 BCE, with the Yamnaya descending from it and spreading the language later. On this account the Anatolian branch, which includes Hittite, did not come from the steppe.
A 2023 study in Science proposed a hybrid model, with an earlier homeland south of the Caucasus and a later branch moving north onto the steppe. Some linguists dispute the 2025 interpretation.
An alternative hypothesis links the origin to Anatolia and the spread of farming.
The relationship between language, genes, and archaeology remains actively debated.
event/indo-european-language-spread.context: The spread happened in the Bronze Age and is tied to the Central Asian Steppe and to horse and wheel technology; see The Wheel.
event/indo-european-language-spread.observer: The Observer notes that a language family can outlive the empires that spread it. A shared tongue is traceable evidence of ancient contact between peoples who no longer remember it.
questions: Which hypothesis for the homeland best fits all the evidence? The 2025 genetic results narrow the steppe hypothesis but do not settle the linguistic argument.

event/industrial-revolution.title: Industrial Revolution
event/industrial-revolution.summary: The Industrial Revolution was the shift, beginning in Britain about 1760, from hand production and animal power to machine production driven by coal and steam.
facts: Key developments included mechanized textile production, the Steam Engine, and railways.
Economic output per person began to rise steadily for the first time in history.
Urban populations grew rapidly, with harsh factory conditions and child labor.
The process spread to continental Europe, North America, and later Asia.
event/industrial-revolution.context: It opens the Industrial Age and connects to Early Modern Period trade and empire; see Technology.
event/industrial-revolution.observer: The Observer calls it the unlocking of stored sunlight: coal and later oil are ancient photosynthesis. For the first time, a species multiplied its available energy by an order of magnitude in a few generations.
questions: Why Britain, and why then?

event/interbreeding-of-homo-sapiens-with.title: Interbreeding of Homo sapiens with Neanderthals and Denisovans
event/interbreeding-of-homo-sapiens-with.summary: Homo sapiens interbred with Neanderthals and with Denisovans, as ancient and present-day DNA show. Most people outside Africa carry about 1 to 2 percent Neanderthal ancestry, and some Oceanian populations carry up to about 5 percent Denisovan ancestry.
facts: Present-day people outside Africa carry about 1 to 2 percent Neanderthal ancestry. Oceanian populations carry up to about 5 percent Denisovan ancestry, and other groups much less.

A 2024 study concluded that most Neanderthal gene flow into modern humans came in one extended episode about 50,500 to 43,500 years ago, lasting about 7,000 years. Denisovan gene flow is dated more loosely, and some studies infer more than one episode.

Denisova 11, a bone fragment from Denisova Cave, belonged to a girl at least 13 years old who lived about 90,000 years ago. Her mother was a Neanderthal and her father a Denisovan, and she is the only known first-generation hybrid.

Some inherited variants were useful: a Denisovan variant of EPAS1 helps Tibetans at high altitude, and archaic variants affect immune genes. Archaic ancestry is scarcer in gene-rich regions, which suggests that many variants were harmful and were removed.
event/interbreeding-of-homo-sapiens-with.context: The interbreeding took place around and after the Out of Africa Dispersal and involved Homo sapiens, Homo neanderthalensis, and the Denisovans. It overlaps the Neanderthal Extinction and the Peopling of Europe by Homo sapiens, and the ancient-DNA methods that revealed it belong to the Genomic Revolution. See Kinship and Society and Science.
event/interbreeding-of-homo-sapiens-with.observer: The Observer notes that boundaries between human groups that later stories treat as fixed were, in the Paleolithic, permeable to the point of shared descent. Other human species live on in most living people as minority ancestry, passed down the kin-lattice from a few thousand years of contact. The reading would weaken if many of these DNA signals proved to come from ancient population structure in Africa instead of interbreeding.
questions: How many separate episodes of interbreeding occurred, and where?
What did the inherited DNA do for those who carried it, and what did it cost them?

event/invention-of-writing.title: Invention of Writing
event/invention-of-writing.summary: Writing was invented independently at least three or four times, first in Mesopotamia about 3400 to 3200 BCE, as a way to record goods and obligations.
facts: The earliest proto-cuneiform tablets from Uruk are accounting records.
Egyptian hieroglyphs appear by about 3200 BCE, and Chinese writing is securely attested by about 1250 BCE.
Mesoamerican writing appears by roughly 600 BCE, and possibly earlier.
Writing systems developed from pictures and tokens toward signs that represent sounds.
event/invention-of-writing.context: Writing begins in the Bronze Age. See Sumerians, Alphabet, and Language and Writing; the essay is The Great Outsourcing of Memory.
event/invention-of-writing.observer: The Observer calls this memory-outsourcing: information moves from the mind to an object. The first users were not poets but accountants, which suggests that the tool arose from a need for trust between strangers.
questions: Did Mesoamerican writing have earlier precursors?

event/last-glacial-maximum.title: Last Glacial Maximum
event/last-glacial-maximum.summary: The Last Glacial Maximum was the most recent time when ice sheets reached their greatest extent, about 26,500 to 19,000 years ago.
facts: Sea level was about 134 meters below today's at its lowest, according to a 2014 global reconstruction.
Ice sheets covered much of northern North America and Europe.
Land exposed by lower seas connected Siberia and Alaska (Beringia) and joined New Guinea and Australia.
Human populations retreated to refuges in some areas and adapted in others.
event/last-glacial-maximum.context: The maximum falls within the Pleistocene Epoch and just precedes the warming that leads to the Holocene Epoch. It affected the Peopling of the Americas.
event/last-glacial-maximum.observer: The Observer sees a bottleneck: the coldest, driest stretch of the species' history preceded the warm stability in which farming and cities appeared.
questions: How did human populations survive the maximum in each region?

event/late-devonian-extinction.title: Late Devonian Extinction
event/late-devonian-extinction.summary: The Late Devonian extinction was a prolonged period of biodiversity loss around 372 to 359 million years ago that heavily affected marine life, especially reef builders.
facts: It comprised at least two main pulses (Kellwasser and Hangenberg).
Around 75 percent of species are estimated to have been lost.
Proposed causes include ocean anoxia, climate change, and the effects of newly spreading land plants on nutrients.
event/late-devonian-extinction.context: It is part of the Paleozoic Era and follows the rise of forests; see Colonization of Land.
event/late-devonian-extinction.observer: The Observer finds it notable that the spread of one group, land plants, is a candidate cause. Success can destabilize the system that supports it.
questions: How large was the role of plants?

event/late-heavy-bombardment.title: Late Heavy Bombardment
event/late-heavy-bombardment.summary: The Late Heavy Bombardment is a hypothesized spike in asteroid impacts on the inner Solar System, roughly 4.1 to 3.8 billion years ago, inferred mainly from radiometric ages of lunar impact rocks.
facts: The hypothesis grew from Apollo-era rock samples whose impact-melt ages cluster near 3.8 to 3.9 billion years.
Some researchers argue the cluster reflects sampling of a few huge basin impacts rather than a real surge in the whole Solar System's impact rate.
The Moon preserves the impact record; Earth's earliest crust has been largely destroyed by plate tectonics and erosion.
Some dynamical models, such as the Nice model, propose that a shift in the giant planets' orbits could have triggered such a surge.
Whether the episode happened at all, and whether it would have sterilized early life, remains debated.
event/late-heavy-bombardment.context: The Late Heavy Bombardment, if real, falls at the end of the Hadean Eon and overlaps the earliest evidence for life, so it bears on Origin of Life. event/late-ordovician-extinction.title: Late Ordovician Extinction
event/late-ordovician-extinction.summary: The Late Ordovician extinction (about 445 to 443 million years ago) is the first of the 'Big Five' mass extinctions, and it eliminated an estimated 85 to 86 percent of species, mostly marine.
facts: It occurred in two pulses.
Glaciation and falling sea levels are the leading proposed causes, followed by rising sea levels and ocean anoxia.
Marine life was hit hardest, since most animals still lived in the sea.

event/latin-american-wars-of-independenc.title: Latin American Wars of Independence
event/latin-american-wars-of-independenc.summary: The Latin American wars of independence (about 1808 to 1826) ended Spanish rule over most of the Americas and created a series of new republics.
facts: They followed Napoleon's invasion of Spain in 1808, which weakened Spanish authority and set off a crisis across the Spanish Empire, though it was not their only cause.
Simón Bolívar and José de San Martín met at Guayaquil on 26 and 27 July 1822. They did not agree on how the new states should be governed, and San Martín then withdrew from the campaigns.
The Battle of Ayacucho on 9 December 1824, won by Antonio José de Sucre, ended effective Spanish resistance in South America.

Bolívar's Gran Colombia was proclaimed in December 1819 and covered what are now Venezuela, Colombia, Panama, and Ecuador. It dissolved in 1830 and 1831, about a decade later, into Venezuela, Ecuador, and New Granada.
event/latin-american-wars-of-independenc.context: The wars were part of the Age of Revolutions, with the Haitian Revolution as an earlier example. See Simón Bolívar.
event/latin-american-wars-of-independenc.observer: The Observer notes that independence in Latin America was won largely by colonial elites, and that many hierarchies of the colonial era outlasted the change of flags.

event/manila-galleon-trade.title: Manila Galleon Trade
event/manila-galleon-trade.summary: From 1565 to 1815, Spanish galleons sailed each year between Manila and Acapulco, carrying Chinese goods to the Americas and American silver to Asia in the first regular trans-Pacific trade.
facts: Andres de Urdaneta found the return route across the North Pacific in 1565.
Manila served as the exchange point where Chinese merchants sold silk and porcelain for silver.
Silver from the Americas, much of it from Potosi, flowed to China.
Goods were carried overland across Mexico and reshipped to Spain.
The trade ended after Mexican independence.

Manila Galleon Trade sits in the Early Modern Period and the region Southeast Asia, and belongs to the theme thread of Trade and Economy.

event/meiji-restoration.title: Meiji Restoration
event/meiji-restoration.summary: The Meiji Restoration was the political and social transformation of Japan that followed the arrival of American warships in 1853 and ended the Tokugawa shogunate in 1868, beginning rapid industrialization.
facts: Commodore Matthew Perry's fleet arrived at Uraga in July 1853, and the Convention of Kanagawa (1854) opened the ports of Shimoda and Hakodate to American ships.
The domains of Choshu and Satsuma formed an alliance against the shogunate in 1866, and on 3 January 1868 imperial rule was 'restored' in the name of Emperor Meiji, then fifteen years old.
The Charter Oath of 1868 promised reform, deliberative assemblies, and the pursuit of knowledge from around the world.
The Iwakura Mission (1871 to 1873) toured the United States and Europe to study institutions.
event/meiji-restoration.context: The restoration ended the Tokugawa Shogunate and made Emperor Meiji the symbol of a modernizing state. Japan adopted Steam Engine and railway technology within a few decades.
event/meiji-restoration.observer: The Observer notes a society that examined the pattern of its neighbors' defeat, in the Opium Wars, and responded by quickly copying what it saw. Some societies learn from the misfortune of others.
questions: Why did Japan avoid the fate of China?

event/messinian-salinity-crisis.title: Messinian Salinity Crisis
event/messinian-salinity-crisis.summary: The Messinian Salinity Crisis was a period from about 5.96 to 5.33 million years ago when the Mediterranean Sea was cut off from the Atlantic and left thick salt deposits on its floor.
facts: Restriction of the Gibraltar gateway caused the Mediterranean to evaporate and deposit more than a million cubic kilometers of salt.
The extent to which the basin dried out completely is debated.
The crisis ended about 5.33 million years ago, when Atlantic water returned through the Gibraltar region.
Some studies propose the refilling was a sudden, catastrophic flood; this is also debated.
The salt deposits lie beneath the present Mediterranean seafloor.
event/messinian-salinity-crisis.context: The crisis shaped the basin around which later Mediterranean civilizations grew; see Mediterranean Basin. It is one of several events in the Cenozoic Era in which tectonic gateways changed ocean circulation. Messinian Salinity Crisis sits in the Cenozoic Era and the region Mediterranean Basin, and belongs to the theme thread of Earth Systems and Life.
event/messinian-salinity-crisis.observer: The Observer notes that the sea on which the species later built empires, cities, and trade routes was once a dry basin. Even the largest stable-looking features of the human world are contingent on gateways that can close.
questions: Did the Mediterranean dry out fully, or only in part?

event/mexican-revolution.title: Mexican Revolution
event/mexican-revolution.summary: The Mexican Revolution (1910 to 1920) overthrew the long rule of Porfirio Díaz and passed through a series of civil wars among revolutionary leaders, producing the Constitution of 1917. Its death toll is uncertain but is usually put at more than a million.
facts: The revolution is dated from 20 November 1910 to 1 December 1920. Porfirio Díaz was forced out and went into exile in France in May 1911.

Francisco I. Madero won the 1911 election and was assassinated in February 1913. A civil war followed among Venustiano Carranza, Francisco 'Pancho' Villa, and Emiliano Zapata, who led the peasant movement in the state of Morelos.
The Constitution of 1917 came out of the revolution and brought far-reaching political and economic change.
Successive revolutionary leaders were assassinated: Madero in 1913, Zapata in 1919, Carranza in 1920, Villa in 1923, and Álvaro Obregón in 1928.

The upheaval is often said to have left more than one million dead. Estimates vary widely, and the figure includes deaths from disease and emigration effects that are hard to separate from combat deaths.
event/mexican-revolution.context: The revolution belongs to the sequence of Latin American upheavals that followed the wars of independence; see Latin American Wars of Independence and Age of Revolutions.
event/mexican-revolution.observer: The Observer notes that a revolution which began by removing one strongman was followed by a decade in which almost every leading figure was killed by another. The 1917 constitution shows how a written story-glue can be drafted amid the fighting and outlast most of those who fought for it.
questions: What was the real death toll, and how much of it was due to disease and famine rather than battle?
How far did the land reforms promised by Zapata's movement actually take effect?

event/mfecane.title: Mfecane
event/mfecane.summary: The Mfecane ('the crushing') is the name given to a period of upheaval, warfare, and migration across southern Africa in the early 19th century, associated with the rise of the Zulu Kingdom.
facts: Several new states emerged, including the Ndebele under Mzilikazi and the Swazi under Sobhuza.
Many adopted Zulu-style military organization.
Population movements reshaped the region and left large areas depopulated in some accounts.
Historians debate the scale, the causes, and the role of Shaka, and some argue that European slave raiding and colonial pressure were also important.

event/middle-pleistocene-transition.title: Middle Pleistocene Transition
event/middle-pleistocene-transition.summary: The Middle Pleistocene Transition was a change in the rhythm of the ice ages between about 1.25 million and 0.7 million years ago. Glacial cycles lengthened from about 41,000 to about 100,000 years, with larger ice sheets and colder glacial stages.
facts: Marine oxygen-isotope records show glacial cycles paced by the 41,000-year tilt cycle until about 1.25 million years ago and dominated by cycles of about 100,000 years by about 0.7 million years ago. Estimates of the start and end vary.
The 100,000-year cycles carry more ice and have a sawtooth shape: slow growth, then rapid melting.

The shift came without a matching change in orbital forcing, so its cause lies inside the climate system. Proposed causes include declining atmospheric carbon dioxide, removal of loose regolith beneath northern ice sheets so that ice grew thicker and more stable, and changes in deep-ocean circulation.
Some reconstructions place a slowdown of deep-ocean circulation near 0.9 million years ago; others find only modest change. Whether the shift was gradual or abrupt is debated.
event/middle-pleistocene-transition.context: The transition falls within the Pleistocene Epoch and Quaternary Period. It changed the rhythm that began with the Onset of Northern Hemisphere Glaciation under the pacing described in Milankovitch Cycles and the Ice Ages, and it set up the later cycles, including the Last Glacial Maximum. It overlaps the range of Homo erectus; no causal link to hominin evolution is established.
event/middle-pleistocene-transition.observer: The Observer files the transition under preconditions: the ice-age world every later people lived in changed its tempo partway through the Quaternary, from a 41,000-year beat to a 100,000-year one. Longer glacial stages mean longer stretches of lower sea level and shrunken habitable ranges, though the Observer does not claim to know how hominins responded. The reading would weaken if the change proved to be an artifact of how sediment records are dated and aligned.
questions: What triggered the change when orbital forcing did not change?
Did longer, harsher glacial stages alter hominin populations in Africa and Eurasia?

event/milankovitch-cycles-and-the-ice-ag.title: Milankovitch Cycles and the Ice Ages
event/milankovitch-cycles-and-the-ice-ag.summary: Milankovitch cycles are slow, regular changes in the shape of Earth's orbit, the tilt of its axis, and the wobble of that axis. They shift how sunlight is spread across latitudes and seasons, and since about 2.6 million years ago they have paced the growth and melting of the Quaternary ice sheets.
facts: The three cycles are eccentricity (orbit shape; about 100,000 and 400,000 years), obliquity (axial tilt, between about 22.1 and 24.5 degrees; 41,000 years), and precession (repeating about every 19,000 to 23,000 years).

Serbian scientist Milutin Milanković calculated between the 1920s and 1940s how these changes alter sunlight by latitude. In 1976 Hays, Imbrie, and Shackleton found the same three periods in oxygen-isotope records from deep-sea sediment cores, which track global ice volume.
The orbital changes alter the distribution of sunlight far more than its yearly total, so ice sheets, ocean circulation, and atmospheric carbon dioxide amplify the effect.

Glacial cycles followed the 41,000-year tilt cycle until about 1.25 million years ago, then lengthened to about 100,000 years; see Middle Pleistocene Transition. Why the 100,000-year cycle dominates is unresolved.
The cycles are far older than the ice ages; what changed about 2.7 million years ago was the climate's response (see Onset of Northern Hemisphere Glaciation).
event/milankovitch-cycles-and-the-ice-ag.context: Milankovitch cycles pace the glacial stages of the Quaternary Period and Pleistocene Epoch, including the Last Glacial Maximum, and the current interglacial, the Holocene Epoch. The Younger Dryas interrupted the last warming. See Earth Systems and Life and Science.
event/milankovitch-cycles-and-the-ice-ag.observer: The Observer notes that the species' whole written record sits inside one warm phase of a cycle set by the geometry of Earth's orbit, a cycle uncovered by pattern-taming from Milanković's sums to the 1976 sediment cores. The Observer treats it as a precondition, not a cause of later history. The reading would weaken if glacial terminations proved to depend more on internal ice-sheet behavior than on orbital pacing.
questions: Why did the 100,000-year cycle come to dominate?
How much do ice sheets, oceans, and carbon dioxide each amplify the response?

event/miocene-great-ape-radiation.title: Miocene Great Ape Radiation
event/miocene-great-ape-radiation.summary: The Miocene great ape radiation was the diversification of apes in Africa, Europe and Asia between about 23 and 7 million years ago. Many more ape forms lived then than survive today.
facts: Early Miocene apes of Africa include Proconsul from Kenya, about 20 million years old. Apes then spread into Europe and Asia, about 17 to 16 million years ago, when a land connection opened.
Later forms include Dryopithecus and Danuvius from Europe, Ouranopithecus from Greece, and Sivapithecus from South Asia, which is related to orangutans. Only about twenty ape species live now.
Molecular studies place the split of the gibbon lineage roughly 17 to 20 million years ago and the orangutan lineage roughly 13 to 16 million years ago, and that of the gorilla lineage later still.
Apes declined in Europe and Asia as the climate cooled and dried, while the ancestors of the African apes and of the hominins survived in Africa.
Whether the last common ancestor of the African apes and humans lived in Africa or in Europe is debated.
event/miocene-great-ape-radiation.context: The Miocene Great Ape Radiation belongs to the Neogene Period and leads to the Divergence of the Hominin Lineage, with early candidates such as Sahelanthropus tchadensis. It runs alongside the Spread of Grasslands. The event belongs to the theme threads of Earth Systems and Life and Science.
event/miocene-great-ape-radiation.observer: The Observer notes that the species belongs to a group once far more diverse than it is now, and that its living relatives are a small remnant. Reading the history of apes from the survivors alone would give a false picture. The reading would weaken if Miocene apes turned out to be mostly close variants of a few forms.

event/modern-climate-change.title: Modern Climate Change
event/modern-climate-change.summary: Modern climate change is the warming of Earth caused mainly by human emissions of greenhouse gases, mostly from burning fossil fuels.
facts: Global surface temperature was about 1.1 degrees Celsius above 1850 to 1900 levels in 2011 to 2020 (IPCC), and has risen further since.

The Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change states that human influence has unequivocally warmed the atmosphere, ocean, and land.
The Paris Agreement, reached on 12 December 2015, set goals of holding warming well below 2 degrees Celsius and pursuing efforts to limit it to 1.5 degrees.

event/moon-landing.title: Moon Landing
event/moon-landing.summary: On 20 July 1969, Apollo 11 astronauts Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin landed on the Moon while Michael Collins orbited above, the first time humans stood on another world.

event/napoleonic-wars.title: Napoleonic Wars

He defeated Austria and Russia at Austerlitz in 1805.
His invasion of Russia in 1812 destroyed most of his Grande Armee, which numbered several hundred thousand men.
He was defeated at Waterloo on 18 June 1815.
The occupation of Spain and Portugal weakened imperial control and helped trigger Latin American independence movements.

event/neanderthal-extinction.title: Neanderthal Extinction
event/neanderthal-extinction.summary: Neanderthals disappeared from the archaeological record of Europe about 41,000 to 39,000 years ago, according to radiocarbon dating of 40 sites. They vanished after several thousand years of overlap with Homo sapiens, and no single cause is agreed.
facts: A 2014 study using improved radiocarbon dating at 40 sites from Spain to Russia found that the Mousterian, the Neanderthal stone-tool industry, ended by about 41,030 to 39,260 calibrated years before present. It estimated an overlap with Homo sapiens of about 2,600 to 5,400 years, a mosaic and not a sudden replacement.
Claims of later survival, such as Gorham's Cave in Gibraltar at about 28,000 years ago, rest on indirect dating and are widely regarded as unproven.
Proposed factors include unstable climate, with a cold, dry spell called Heinrich Stadial 4 around 40,000 years ago; competition with Homo sapiens; disease; and small, inbred populations.
Neanderthal DNA survives in present-day people outside Africa at about 1 to 2 percent, so some Neanderthal ancestry was absorbed; see Interbreeding of Homo sapiens with Neanderthals and Denisovans.
A very large eruption in Italy about 40,000 years ago, the Campanian Ignimbrite Eruption, has been suggested as a factor. Its effect on Neanderthals is disputed.
event/neanderthal-extinction.context: The extinction ends the Homo neanderthalensis lineage near the boundary between the Middle Paleolithic and the Upper Paleolithic. It overlaps the Peopling of Europe by Homo sapiens. See Kinship and Society and Earth Systems and Life.
event/neanderthal-extinction.observer: The Observer treats this as a case in which the species has a stake in the answer, and is wary of the tidy version in which one group beat another. The evidence supports thousands of years of contact, some interbreeding, small Neanderthal populations, and hard climate. The reading would weaken if a well-dated site showed direct conflict or a sudden collapse.

event/nuclear-age.title: Nuclear Age
event/nuclear-age.summary: The Nuclear Age began on 16 July 1945 with the first nuclear weapon test, followed by the bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki on 6 and 9 August.
facts: Nuclear weapons rely on Nuclear Fission (later also fusion).
The Cold War produced arsenals of tens of thousands of warheads; about 12,000 remain today.
Nuclear deterrence, arms-control treaties, and nonproliferation shaped world politics.
Nuclear power also provides a share of the world's electricity.
event/nuclear-age.context: The Nuclear Age sits within the Information Age. See Albert Einstein and Marie Curie for related science.
event/nuclear-age.observer: The Observer notes that the species has, since 1945, held the technical means to end its own history. The fact that it has survived so far is itself a subject of study.
questions: Which factors best explain the absence of nuclear use since 1945?

event/onset-of-northern-hemisphere-glaci.title: Onset of Northern Hemisphere Glaciation
event/onset-of-northern-hemisphere-glaci.summary: The onset of Northern Hemisphere glaciation was the growth of large ice sheets across North America and Eurasia about 2.7 million years ago. It began the repeating glacial and interglacial cycles of the Quaternary Period.
facts: Ice-rafted debris in North Atlantic seafloor sediments becomes widespread about 2.7 million years ago, and loess deposits begin to build up on the Chinese Loess Plateau about 2.6 million years ago.
Smaller ice sheets existed earlier in the Northern Hemisphere; the change was a large expansion, not a first appearance of ice.

Proposed causes include a slow decline in atmospheric carbon dioxide through the Pliocene, changes in ocean circulation, and mountain uplift that altered atmospheric flow. The closure of the Isthmus of Panama is a candidate cause, but its timing is debated; see Closure of the Isthmus of Panama.
The first cycles followed variations in the tilt of Earth's axis, with a period of about 41,000 years.
event/onset-of-northern-hemisphere-glaci.context: The Onset of Northern Hemisphere Glaciation comes near the end of the Neogene Period and leads into the Quaternary Period, and it builds on the earlier cooling of the Eocene-Oligocene Transition. The event belongs to the Cenozoic Era and the theme thread of Earth Systems and Life.
event/onset-of-northern-hemisphere-glaci.observer: The Observer notes that the world every human society has known is one of repeating ice ages, which began only about 2.7 million years ago after a slow decline in carbon dioxide and perhaps a rearrangement of ocean gateways. The Observer takes this as context, not cause: what it did to the making of humans is a separate and unsettled question. The reading would weaken if the carbon dioxide decline proved too small to explain the change.
questions: What combination of carbon dioxide decline and ocean change tipped the climate into glacial cycles?
How did the new climate rhythm affect early hominins?

event/onset-of-plate-tectonics.title: Onset of Plate Tectonics
event/onset-of-plate-tectonics.summary: The onset of plate tectonics is the start of the motion of rigid plates of Earth's outer shell, with ocean floor recycled into the mantle at subduction zones. Proposed dates range from before 4 billion to about 0.8 billion years ago, and the question remains one of the most disputed in Earth science.
facts: Plate tectonics moves about a dozen large plates and recycles ocean floor at subduction zones. Earth is the only planet known to have it.

Proposed onsets include before 4.0 billion years ago, about 3.2 billion years ago, about 2.5 billion years ago and about 0.8 billion years ago. Some researchers argue for a gradual transition from a rigid outer lid, or for episodic subduction long before modern-style plate motion.

Blueschists, which form in cold subduction zones, and ultra-high-pressure metamorphic rocks appear in the record only after about 0.8 billion years ago, which some geologists read as a marker of modern-style subduction.
Alfred Wegener proposed continental drift in 1912, and plate tectonics gained wide acceptance in the 1960s.
Plate tectonics builds continents and recycles carbon; whether it was needed for a long-lived biosphere is debated.
event/onset-of-plate-tectonics.context: The Onset of Plate Tectonics is tied to the growth of continents in the Archean Eon and to the Earliest Continental Crust. Its later effects include the Breakup of Pangaea and the Collision of India and Asia. The event belongs to the theme threads of Earth Systems and Life and Science.
event/onset-of-plate-tectonics.observer: The Observer notes that Earth's surface has recycled its own earliest evidence, so when the process began may be settled only indirectly. Some geologists treat plate tectonics as a precondition for a long-lived biosphere, and the Observer keeps that as an open hypothesis. It reads the current disagreement as information about the limits of the record, and it would weaken if a reliable early rock record were found.
questions: When did plate tectonics begin, and was the change gradual or sudden?
Was plate tectonics required for a long-lived biosphere?

event/opening-of-the-silk-roads.title: Opening of the Silk Roads
event/opening-of-the-silk-roads.summary: The Silk Roads were overlapping overland and sea routes linking East Asia, South Asia, Central Asia, and the Mediterranean, which grew from the second century BCE.
facts: Missions by the Han envoy Zhang Qian, around 138 to 126 BCE, are often taken as a starting point.
Goods included silk, horses, glass, spices, and paper; ideas and religions such as Buddhism spread along them.
Disease also traveled the routes; see Black Death.
The name 'Silk Road' was coined in 1877 by the German geographer Ferdinand von Richthofen.
event/opening-of-the-silk-roads.context: The routes link East Asia, the Central Asian Steppe, South Asia and the Mediterranean Basin, and grew under the Han Dynasty and later the Mongol Empire.
event/opening-of-the-silk-roads.observer: The Observer treats the Silk Roads as an exchange-web with no owner. Very few travelers went the whole way; goods and ideas moved through chains of intermediaries.
questions: How much long-distance trade was in luxury goods versus everyday goods?

event/opium-wars.title: Opium Wars
event/opium-wars.summary: The Opium Wars were two conflicts between Qing China and Britain (and, in the second, France) over trade and diplomatic relations, fought 1839 to 1842 and 1856 to 1860, which opened China to Western commerce on unequal terms.
facts: The Treaty of Nanking (1842) ceded Hong Kong Island to Britain and opened five treaty ports: Canton, Amoy, Foochow, Ningpo, and Shanghai.
The Convention of Beijing (1860) gave Britain the Kowloon peninsula and granted foreign powers permanent diplomatic presence in Beijing.
It also legalized the opium trade and gave Christians the right to own property and preach.
The wars are remembered in China as the start of a 'century of humiliation'.
event/opium-wars.context: The wars weakened the Qing Dynasty just before the Taiping Rebellion. Industrial-age naval and firearm superiority, from the Industrial Revolution, decided the outcome.
event/opium-wars.observer: The Observer notes a trade war in a literal sense: a state fought to keep a product from its own people, and lost to a state that fought to sell it. Exchange-webs are not always fair.
questions: How much did opium trade shape the Qing decline compared with internal problems?

event/origin-of-bipedalism.title: Origin of Bipedalism
event/origin-of-bipedalism.summary: Habitual upright walking arose in the human lineage in Africa between roughly 7 and 4 million years ago. It is the earliest hallmark of the hominins, millions of years older than large brains or stone tools, but its starting point and cause are disputed.
facts: Sahelanthropus tchadensis, from Chad and about 7 million years old, has a skull base that suggests upright posture. A 2022 study of a femur argued for habitual bipedalism, but others dispute this, and its status as a hominin is debated.
Orrorin tugenensis, from Kenya and about 6 million years old, is known from thigh bones read as evidence of bipedality; the reading is controversial.

Ardipithecus ramidus, from Ethiopia and about 4.4 million years old, had a pelvis combining climbing and walking features and a grasping big toe. How well it walked is debated, and its excavators read its site as woodland, not open savanna.
Footprints at Laetoli, Tanzania, about 3.66 million years old and attributed to Australopithecus afarensis, are the earliest direct record of upright walking.
Proposed reasons include energy efficiency, carrying food or infants, heat regulation, and feeding from thin branches. None is agreed.
event/origin-of-bipedalism.context: The origin of bipedalism follows the Divergence of the Hominin Lineage and falls within the Neogene Period of the Cenozoic Era. It precedes the Emergence of the Genus Homo and the Oldowan Stone Tools by millions of years. See Earth Systems and Life and Science.
event/origin-of-bipedalism.observer: The Observer notes that the species' ancestors walked upright for millions of years before they had large brains or made recognizable tools, so the posture was not an adaptation for those things, and nothing in the record shows it heading toward them. The Observer reads it as a precondition: hands freed from walking could later carry and make. The reading would weaken if the earliest claimed bipeds proved to be apes with independently evolved postures.
questions: Was Sahelanthropus a habitual biped, and was it a hominin?
Did upright walking begin on the ground or in the trees?

event/origin-of-birds.title: Origin of Birds
event/origin-of-birds.summary: Birds evolved from small feathered theropod dinosaurs in the Jurassic, with the earliest bird-like fossils about 160 to 150 million years old. Birds are the only dinosaur lineage that survived to the present.
facts: Birds share many features with theropod dinosaurs, including hollow bones, a wishbone and a three-fingered hand. Feathered non-avian dinosaurs found in China from the 1990s onward strengthened the link.
Feathers arose before flight, probably for insulation or display. The theropod Anchiornis, about 160 million years old, and Archaeopteryx, about 150 million years old, both had feathered wings.
Early Cretaceous fossils from China, about 125 million years old, show many forms of early birds, including toothless-beaked Confuciusornis.
How flight began, from the ground up or from the trees down, is debated, and some small feathered dinosaurs had four wings.
Only the lineage of modern birds survived the Cretaceous-Paleogene Extinction, and living birds diversified after it.
event/origin-of-birds.context: The Origin of Birds lies within the Jurassic Period and the Mesozoic Era and belongs to the story of the Dinosaurs. The event belongs to the theme threads of Earth Systems and Life and Science.
event/origin-of-birds.observer: The Observer notes that a category as familiar as bird sits inside a category as remote as dinosaur, a reminder that names for kinds of animals are cuts across a continuous line of descent. The reading concerns naming only, and it would not be affected by the debate over where flight began.
questions: Where in theropod evolution did powered flight first arise?
Which Jurassic fossils count as birds and which as close relatives?

event/origin-of-eukaryotes.title: Origin of Eukaryotes
event/origin-of-eukaryotes.summary: Eukaryotes, the cells with nuclei and internal organelles from which all animals, plants, and fungi are built, arose roughly 2 billion years ago, with very wide uncertainty about the date.
facts: Mitochondria descend from bacteria taken into a host cell, a process called endosymbiosis, which is widely accepted.
Chloroplasts likewise descend from cyanobacteria that became resident in some eukaryotic cells.
Genomic studies place the host cell within the Archaea, with the Asgard archaea often named as the closest relatives.

The oldest unambiguous eukaryote fossils, large organic-walled microfossils, are more than 1.65 billion years old; older candidates such as Grypania (about 1.87 billion years) are less convincing than younger, larger forms.
Molecular-clock estimates for the last common ancestor of living eukaryotes vary widely.
event/origin-of-eukaryotes.context: The origin of eukaryotes followed the oxygen rise of the Great Oxidation Event and made large multicellular bodies possible, leading eventually to the Cambrian Explosion. Origin of Eukaryotes sits in the Proterozoic Eon and the region Planet-wide, and belongs to the theme thread of Earth Systems and Life and Science.
event/origin-of-eukaryotes.observer: The Observer notes that complex life arose through a merger rather than a single lineage inventing new parts alone. Cooperation between unlike partners sits at the base of every body, including the human one. A different origin would be indicated if strong evidence showed the organelles were built internally without symbiosis.
questions: Did the host cell acquire the mitochondrion before or after gaining complexity?
How old is the last eukaryotic common ancestor?

event/origin-of-homo-sapiens.title: Origin of Homo sapiens
event/origin-of-homo-sapiens.summary: Anatomically modern humans, Homo sapiens, emerged in Africa by about 300,000 years ago through a gradual, continent-wide process.
facts: The Jebel Irhoud fossils in Morocco are about 315,000 years old (315 plus or minus 34 thousand years) and show a modern face and teeth with a more archaic braincase.
Fossils from Omo Kibish (Ethiopia) are at least 233,000 years old, dated against a volcanic ash layer.
Some scholars describe the process as 'African multiregionalism', with several connected populations contributing.
The regional tag here is approximate: Jebel Irhoud is in North Africa, while the other main sites are in East and southern Africa.
event/origin-of-homo-sapiens.context: The origin belongs to the Pleistocene Epoch and precedes the Out of Africa Dispersal. See Homo sapiens.
event/origin-of-homo-sapiens.observer: The Observer notes that the species' origin is not a single place or moment. It is a widespread, interbreeding population that became recognizably modern over tens of thousands of years.
questions: Was there one core population, or many linked ones?
